papers.title: Scenario Synthetic Dataset Creation for Smart Mobility: Seamless Coverage of Normal and Critical Conditions
papers.authors: Liron Ahmeti, Klara Dolos, Conrad Meyer, Andreas Attenberger, Rudolf Hackenberg
papers.abstract: This work introduces a configurable, CARLA-based testbench that generates synchronized vehicle dynamics, multi-sensor feeds, and CAN traffic for forensic analysis of autonomous driving incidents. By overlaying layered YAML configurations, it supports blue-team data collection of nominal scenarios, red-team fault injections (e.g., sensor dropouts or CAN replay), and flexible accident replays with environmental and control disturbances. Physics-informed noise models simulate rain, snow, and fog effects on LiDAR and radar sensors, while a virtual CAN network implements SecOC authentication and TimeSync. The resulting synthetic dataset—including time-aligned point clouds, images, Controller Area Network traces, and Event Data Recorder dumps—enables systematic evaluation of intrusion-detection systems and kinematic reconstructions without real-world risks.

papers.title: The Omani Way: Muscat’s Navigation of Iran–Israel Rivalry
papers.authors: Giorgio Cafiero
papers.abstract: This paper examines Oman’s foreign policy amid the escalating US-Israel-Iran conflict. Traditionally a neutral diplomatic mediator, Oman faces unprecedented challenges as Tehran’s aggression targets Duqm, Salalah, and Sohar—ports central to the Sultanate’s Vision 2040 economic diversification strategy. The analysis explores how Oman balances its long-standing relationship with Iran against its security partnership with the United States, while navigating domestic societal dynamics marked by rising anti-Western sentiment and support for the Palestinian cause. The paper argues that despite heightened threat perceptions and frustration with Washington’s regional policies, Oman will continue pursuing a pragmatic, balanced foreign policy. Muscat seeks to preserve its unique role as a diplomatic bridge between adversaries, maintain stable ties with both Tehran and Western allies, and protect its economic development agenda. However, Iran’s direct strikes on Omani infrastructure and the fundamental shifts in Gulf security architecture pose serious tests to the sustainability of Oman’s traditional approach to regional diplomacy.

papers.title: Recent advances in multi-agent human trajectory prediction: A comprehensive review
papers.authors: Céline Finet, Stephane Da Silva Martins, Jean-Bernard Hayet, Ioannis Karamouzas, Sylvie Le Hégarat‐Mascle, Julien Pettré, Emanuel Aldea
papers.abstract: With the emergence of powerful data-driven methods in human trajectory prediction (HTP), gaining a finer understanding of multi-agent interactions lies within hand’s reach, with important implications in areas such as social robot navigation, autonomous driving, and crowd modeling. This survey reviews some of the most recent advancements in deep learning-based multi-agent trajectory prediction, focusing on studies published between 2020 and 2025. We categorize the existing methods based on their architectural design, their input representations, and their overall prediction strategies. Furthermore, we highlight key challenges and future research directions in multi-agent HTP.

papers.title: Performance Evaluation of Space and Underwater Robots using the WSM Method
papers.authors: Chandraseka Raja
papers.abstract: Space and underwater robots explore environments that are difficult or dangerous for humans to access. Space systems, including planetary rovers and robotic manipulators, support surface investigations, space-station activities, and satellite maintenance. Underwater platforms, such as autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) and remotely operated vehicles (ROVs), enable deep-ocean exploration, seabed mapping, environmental monitoring, inspection, and construction. Examples include Bluefin-21, HUGIN 4500, CR-2, REMUS 6000, and Qianlong-1. This study examines the design, operation, and applications of these systems, focusing on shape and general arrangement, power supplies, underwater communication, and navigation and positioning technologies. Although they operate in different environments, both types face harsh conditions, communication limitations or delays, and navigation challenges. Advances in artificial intelligence, sensors, autonomous control, and machine learning can improve their reliability, efficiency, and decision-making. The research combines theoretical modeling, computer simulation, and experimental testing. Robotic designs and algorithms are evaluated under simulated extreme conditions and validated through controlled trials, including underwater test sites and space-analogue missions. Collected data are analyzed to improve autonomy, communication, navigation, and overall performance through iterative testing. The findings aim to support safer future robotic missions and expand scientific understanding of remote environments. In the comparative table, Hash Table ranks first, whereas Graph ranks last.

papers.title: Intent Representation and Human Distraction Modulate the Effects of Legible Robot Motion in Hallway Navigation
papers.authors: Pranav Goyal, Andrew Stratton, Christoforos Mavrogiannis
papers.abstract: Legibility in human-robot interaction (HRI) is often described as the property of robot motion that enables an observer to confidently and quickly infer the robot’s intent. Mature frameworks exist for generating legible motion in front of static observers, typically by making the robot’s destination apparent as early as possible. Social robot navigation in public spaces, however, presents a different challenge: pedestrians are themselves in motion, often with divided attention, and must coordinate with the robot in real time. In such encounters, where the robot is ultimately headed may matter less to a pedestrian than how it intends to pass them. This raises two questions: which aspect of intent should legible motion convey, and does legibility remain beneficial when pedestrians are not fully attentive to the robot? We address these questions in the ubiquitous and demanding scenario of hallway navigation, through two controlled user studies comparing multiple legibility formulations implemented within a shared model predictive control framework. Study 1 ( N = 45) compares destination-based and passing-side intent representations, showing that the latter, particularly when adaptively updated, allows for smoother human motion and is perceived as more competent and less mentally and physically demanding than the former. Study 2 ( N = 45) examines the effect of pedestrian attention, demonstrating that legible motion supports smooth human motion even under distraction, although this benefit is not consistently reflected in subjective ratings. Together, these findings suggest that effective legible motion in social robot navigation benefits from interaction-level intent representations that support coordination, with some effects persisting even when human attention is divided. Code is available at https://github.com/fluentrobotics/Legible_MPPI and footage from our experiments at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P5O5BwfcUCo .

papers.title: Human Centric Embodied Intelligence for Soft Wearable Robotics
papers.authors: Rainier F. Natividad, Chen‐Hua Yeow
papers.abstract: Soft wearable robots have evolved rapidly from proof‐of‐concept devices into promising platforms for rehabilitation, occupational assistance, and human augmentation. As the field matures, its central challenge extends beyond developing softer materials and more capable actuators to integrating sensing, intelligence, and human adaptation into systems that users can wear comfortably, trust, and benefit from over long periods. This transition motivates the concept of human centric embodied intelligence (HCEI). In HCEI, intelligence emerges from the coupled human–robot system, through the interaction of morphology, multimodal sensing, adaptive cognition, compliant actuation, and the wearer's own physiological and behavioral adaptation. To organize this perspective, we introduce the perception–cognition–actuation–augmentation (PCAA) framework. It proposes that design start from the augmentation objective, the change sought in the wearer's function, and that the requirements on perception, cognition, and actuation be derived from that objective rather than from the actuating mechanism. Using this framework, we review advances in soft materials, wearable sensing, artificial intelligence, actuation, human–robot interaction, digital twins, clinical translation, manufacturing, regulation, and ethics, and trace how these interdependent components together shape long‐term personalization and real‐world deployment. The review aims to guide future research, encourage interdisciplinary collaboration, and speed the translation of soft wearable robots toward personalized, predictive, and human‐centric wearable intelligence.

papers.title: Agentic Robotics: Redefining Robot Perception, Planning, Control, and Multi-Agent Autonomy through Agentic Super Intelligence
papers.authors: Ranjan Sapkota, Manoj Karkee, Seyedali Mirjalili
papers.abstract: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI) is emerging as a system-level paradigm that reorganizes robotic autonomy beyond conventional perception-planning-control pipelines. This report traces the evolution from autonomy to agency and introduces a layered capability model connecting machine learning, generative AI, embodied foundation models, AI agents, and coordinated multi-agent systems. We define "Agentic AI in robotics" at the system level and synthesize an architecture integrating persistent perceive-reason-act-verify reflect loops, structured memory, tool invocation, and safety gates. Furthermore, this study examines agentic perception through goal-conditioned sensing and Vision-Language-Action alignment; agentic planning through goal decomposition, multimodal world modeling, and reflective replanning; and agentic control through semantic-to-physical translation, adaptive execution, verification, recovery, and multi-robot coordination. Existing robotics benchmarks are reframed using metrics for task competence, persistence, recovery, generalization, continual learning, coordination, latency, and deployability. Key limitations include hallucinated reasoning, memory drift, sim-to-real gaps, computational overhead, integration debt, and governance risks. Future agentic robotics will increasingly combine neuro-symbolic reasoning, physics-aware models, calibrated autonomy, formal verification, and governed multi-agent collaboration, enabling scalable, explainable, resilient, and trustworthy robotic systems.

papers.title: What makes a laboratory self-driving? Mapping the SDL terminology landscape and introducing the FLEx categorization framework
papers.authors: Alexander Böser, Kjell Kochale, Patrick Courtney, Thorsten Teutenberg, Florian Boser, Guangqi Wu, Nikhil Deshpande, Christian P. Haas
papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are increasingly used to accelerate experimentation across chemistry, materials science, biotechnology, and related fields. Yet, the rapid development of autonomous experimentation has produced a fragmented terminology landscape in which overlapping terms, including autonomous laboratories, materials acceleration platforms, and robot scientists, are applied inconsistently. This complicates comparisons between systems and obscures what constitutes scientific autonomy. Here, we examine the definitions, historical development, disciplinary associations, and usage patterns of SDLs and related concepts. We further review existing approaches to categorizing autonomous laboratory systems and show that many rely on characteristics such as hardware complexity, system architecture, or human involvement that are difficult to apply consistently across disciplines and technologies. To provide a technology-independent alternative, we introduce the Feedback Loop Extent (FLEx) framework. FLEx classifies systems according to how far experimental feedback reaches into the scientific process, progressing from scripted execution without a scientific feedback loop to parameter optimization, autonomous experiment planning, hypothesis formulation, and scientific goal formulation. Applying FLEx to representative published systems shows that most contemporary SDLs autonomously plan experiments within human-defined objectives, whereas few demonstrably formulate hypotheses and none unambiguously reformulate broader scientific goals. FLEx provides a common language for distinguishing automation from different forms of autonomy and enables more transparent comparison and reporting of current and future SDLs.

papers.title: User-initiated and system-prompted human feedback in human-robot collaboration: effects on trust in robots
papers.authors: Viktor Werbilo, Andreas Poppele, Andrea Vogt, Alexandra Coroiu, Carl Wedepohl, Ritu Ahmed, Sven Hallerbach
papers.abstract: Feedback is an important interaction channel in human–robot collaboration (HRC), yet feedback solicitation may affect users independently of whether their feedback changes robot behavior. This between-subjects study investigated how user-initiated and system-prompted feedback influence short-term trust development and perceived safety in a virtual industrial collaboration task. Forty-eight participants were assigned to either a system-prompted condition ( n = 23 ) , in which feedback was requested at predefined task milestones, or a user-initiated condition ( n = 25 ) , in which feedback could be provided at self-selected moments. Trust was assessed before and after the interaction, while perceived safety was measured afterward. A mixed ANCOVA revealed a significant time-by-condition interaction: trust increased in the system-prompted condition, compared to the user-initiated condition. Perceived safety did not differ between conditions. These findings suggest that feedback solicitation may function as an interaction-design feature that may shape short-term trust and feedback coverage under stable robot behavior.

papers.title: Thermal influences on interpersonal space: Effects of environmental and visually induced temperature
papers.authors: Laura Battistel, Zubin Choudhary, Gerd Bruder, Gregory F. Welch, Massimiliano Zampini, Riccardo Parin
papers.abstract: Interpersonal space (IPS), the distance people prefer to maintain from others, is a fundamental component of social behaviour. Here we tested whether ambient temperature, delivered as a physical manipulation or conveyed by visual cues in immersive virtual reality, modulates IPS. A total of 120 adults (39% female, age 32 ± 9 years) completed a standard comfort-distance task under a neutral baseline and additional thermal contexts. In the physical manipulation, participants were assigned to extreme conditions (8 °C - 38 °C) or mild conditions (18 °C - 28 °C). In the visual manipulation, participants completed the task at constant room temperature (21 °C) while immersed in either a virtual outdoor or indoor thermal scene. At the individual level, physical temperature significantly altered IPS in 70% of the physical sample, whereas visually conveyed temperature altered IPS in 20% of the visual sample, demonstrating that thermal context can reshape proxemic preferences for a substantial subset of individuals. At the group level, physical temperature produced gender-dependent shifts in mean IPS, with men increasing IPS in warmer conditions (warm vs neutral: p < 0.01, Cohen's f = 0.30), while women showed no consistent behaviour shifts. Visually conveyed thermal context produced smaller average shifts, matched the same directional pattern and emerged only in men as for the physical manipulation ( p < 0.01, Cohen's f = 0.30). Together, these findings highlight that thermal context should be taken into account in social settings to preserve interpersonal comfort, both in public spaces and in XR environments.

papers.title: System Trust or Self-Efficacy? Behavioral Intention Toward Wearable Devices in Immersive Embodied VR for Upper-Limb Training: An Integrated Cognitive-Affective Perspective
papers.authors: Yujun Chen, Zheng Xu, Tao Yang
papers.abstract: Although virtual reality (VR) and motion capture technologies are increasingly being applied in rehabilitation training, existing research has largely focused on analyzing users’ experience. The underlying mechanisms of cognitive-emotional trust resulting from the synergistic effects of technological features and in-depth gamification design remain unclear. This study aimed to examine the determinants that influenced behavior in immersive VR upper-limb training by integrating the stimulus-biological-response and cognitive-emotional-behavioral models. Furthermore, we combined technical features, the situational learning theory, and two-dimensional trust (based on the trust and self-efficacy theories) from an attribution perspective. We developed an immersive VR training system and obtained experimental data from 280 users. Analysis employed Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), Necessary Configuration Analysis (NConfA), and Artificial Neural Networks (ANN). Results revealed that Environmental Embeddedness had a significantly greater effect on the situational cognition dimension than Embodied Interactivity. However, Perceived Incentives had no significant effect on Affective Trust in Technology. NConfA results identified four necessary configurations that promoted high levels of behavioral intention. Furthermore, ANN findings illustrated strong non-linear relationships between Immersion, learning motivation, and task-specific self-efficacy, demonstrating Immersion’s crucial role in the overall formation mechanism. Based on a cognitive-affective trust perspective, this study provides guidance for all relevant stakeholders: Immersion and interactive experiences should be strengthened to promote self-efficacy, thereby fostering behavioral intentions.

papers.title: Sensing Together: A Transdisciplinary Co-Design Study of the VR Baby Experience
papers.authors: Heide Karen Lukosch, Ngaroma Williams, Tony Walls, Niki Newman, Rodrigo Dias-Takase, Elizabeth Jayne White
papers.abstract: This work reports on the ongoing co-design of an immersive learning environment that places student teachers and healthcare students in embodied encounters with a virtual infant. Drawing on autoethnographic engagement with a transdisciplinary design team, we examine how the process is shaped by whanaungatanga, the Māori relational principle of connection and reciprocity, as it meets Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) practice, early childhood pedagogy, and paediatric health expertise. We report early findings on three themes of designing presence, translating across knowledge worlds, and the design team as relational practice, and reflect critically on the limits of our current process, including its restricted end-user and Māori community involvement. We position this work as transdisciplinary co-design rather than end-user co-design in the canonical HCI sense, and outline planned user studies with healthcare and ECE communities as the next phase of this research.

papers.title: Robot-assisted versus laparoscopic-assisted radical right hemicolectomy: short-term and 5-year outcomes in 2057 cases
papers.authors: Taiyuan Li, Ruichen Zhou, Penghui He, Yahang Liang, Feng Xiao, Wenjun Hu, Dongning Liu
papers.abstract: Background With the increasing application of robotic surgical systems in the field of gastrointestinal surgery, their technical advantages in achieving precise dissection and stable manipulation have become increasingly evident in clinical practice. This study aims to compare the perioperative outcomes and long-term survival outcomes of robot-assisted radical right hemicolectomy (RA) and laparoscopic-assisted radical right hemicolectomy (LA) for colon cancer.Methods This study is a retrospective analysis; a total of 2057 patients with right-sided colon cancer were enrolled from the First Affiliated Hospital of Nanchang University between 2015 and 2020. No significant differences were observed in baseline characteristics between the two groups. The primary endpoints of this study were 5-year cancer-specific survival (CSS) and disease-free survival (DFS) after surgery, while the secondary endpoints were perioperative outcomes.Results The RA group was associated with significantly higher 5-year CSS and DFS than the LA group (CSS: 79.9% vs. 74.6%, p = 0.005; DFS: 74.2% vs. 67.3%, p = 0.001). Surgical approach was an independent prognostic factor for both CSS and DFS (CSS: hazard ratio (HR) = 0.75, p = 0.008; DFS: HR = 0.75, p = 0.002). For perioperative outcomes, the RA group was associated with less intraoperative blood loss, more lymph nodes harvested (both p < 0.001), and a lower complication rate (p = 0.001).Conclusions RA was associated with more favourable perioperative outcomes and better long-term survival than LA.

papers.title: Not Coded Dopamine: What Would Count as a Machine That Feels
papers.authors: Abdelrahman El Sayad
papers.abstract: In July 2026 I spent two days asking a large language model to find me a sentient machine I could put into a robot, and I rejected every answer it gave. This paper turns that rejection into a test. A system earns the right to be discussed as a candidate for feeling only if it meets four conditions. It must be embodied, sensing and acting through a body of its own. It must run a homeostatic economy with real stakes, in which internal variables have to be held in range for the system to go on existing, and in which the system itself does the holding. It must contain no labeled shortcuts: no component may carry the name of a feeling or a drive unless removing that component removes the function the name describes. And it must persist, carrying its state and its history forward in time without a human reloading it. I score the current candidate builds against these conditions: a vision language action model on a robot arm, spiking neural networks, a whole connectome simulation in a toy robot, living neuron cultures and brain organoids, and fungal computing, including hybrids where the record supports them, with the fungal hybrid examined in depth. None passes. I then state the harder problem plainly. No accepted test for machine consciousness exists, so passing my four conditions would not prove inner experience either. The conditions are gates for taking a claim seriously. They are not a detector. I close with the observations that would change my mind.

papers.title: Material Prompts: Exploring Human-AI Interaction in Emerging Robotic Fabrication Contexts
papers.authors: Anthony Franze, Wei Win Loy, Jimmy Vermeulen, Müge Belek Fıalho Teıxeıra, Glenda Amayo Caldwell, Yuan Liu, Vincent Moug
papers.abstract: Robotic 3D printing is emerging as a socio-technical scenario for exploring human-AI interactions because it brings people, machines and evolving material conditions into continuous negotiation. As deposited materials shift, sag, accumulate, or behave unexpectedly, designers may need to interpret changing conditions and decide whether, when, and how to intervene during fabrication. While some research has begun to explore AI support for additive manufacturing, less is known about how people should interact with AI during unfolding, materially consequential processes. This creates a need to explore interaction models that support situated judgement and negotiation among people, AI systems, machines, and materials. In this half-day workshop, we ask the OzCHI community: how might AI support human decision-making as robotic 3D printing processes unfold? Participants will explore this question through speculative activities that progress from hands-on collaborative making to simulated AI assistance and to a low-fidelity enactment of a robotic 3D-printing scenario. Rather than testing a working AI system, the session uses speculative role-play as a design probe to examine how people interpret, question, reject, and build on AI suggestions as material conditions evolve. Workshop insights will be synthesised into a preliminary vocabulary of interaction patterns and communication needs to inform the design of future AI-assisted fabrication interfaces and workflows.

papers.title: Markerless three-dimensional biomechanical analysis of manual flexible ureteroscopy: experience-related differences in wrist load during lower-calyx access
papers.authors: Satoshi Kobayashi, Keiji Tsukino, Mikifumi Koura, Masaki Shiota
papers.abstract: Purpose To quantify upper-limb kinematics and estimated biomechanical load (a kinematics-derived load proxy, not measured muscle force) during simulated manual flexible ureteroscopy (fURS) using markerless 3D pose estimation, testing whether experience-related differences concentrate in lower-calyx access. Methods Eighteen urologists (10 experts, 8 novices) performed a phantom task: renal pelvis to upper, middle and lower calyx, returning to the pelvis between calyces. 3D landmarks from smartphone video (MediaPipe Pose) were converted to joint angles, jerk and inverse-dynamics load estimates. Primary outcomes were right-wrist force, jerk and angle in the lower-calyx phase; others were exploratory, analysed with participant-level Welch tests, Hedges g, 95% CIs, Holm correction and a mixed model for group × phase interaction. Results Procedure time was longer in novices (115.5 vs 61.5 s). In the lower-calyx phase, novices showed higher right-wrist force (1.87 vs 1.16 N; Holm p = 0.026), jerk (Holm p = 0.020) and angle (31.6° vs 24.9°; Holm p = 0.026), with no upper-calyx differences; force and jerk showed significant group × phase interactions (p = 0.004, 0.007) but angle did not (p = 0.35). Force, jerk and dispersion correlated strongly with movement speed (ρ = 0.93–0.99), and group differences were attenuated after speed adjustment. Conclusion In this simulator study, experience-related differences in estimated wrist load emerged mainly during lower-calyx access, whereas wrist angle differed throughout, pinpointing an ergonomic target. Because estimates were kinematics-derived and not EMG-validated, findings are hypothesis-generating; correlating them with physiological muscle activity is an important next step for robot-assisted ureteroscopy design.

papers.title: LCA of smart building energy systems and installations from a Nordic perspective
papers.authors: Bojana Petrovic, Marianne Kjendseth Wiik, Lina Morkūnaitė, Susana G. Sanfelix, Shahab Zangi, Andrea Ferrantelli, Eduard Petlenkov, Ali Reza Yaghoubi
papers.abstract: The upcoming revision of the Energy Performance of Buildings Directive (EPBD) will require reporting of the whole life-cycle global warming potential (GWP) for new buildings from 2028 at the European level. In the Nordic countries, several frontrunners have already introduced national climate declaration requirements for new buildings. The focus was primarily on embodied emissions from building materials. However, buildings also comprise a wide range of building energy systems (BES) and technical installations, which contribute to the overall impact. Despite their importance, there is currently a lack of research regarding these building components. Therefore, this paper presents greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of BES and technical installations by using GWP-total climate data. The embodied GHG emissions from the production of air handling units (AHU), lighting systems, cables, cable joints/connectors, LED kits, panel radiators, and transformers are presented as minimum, median, mean, and maximum values. The analysis is based on a dataset of 1,622 environmental product declarations (EPDs) collected across the Nordic countries. The dataset is largely composed of products manufactured in Sweden (44%), followed by Norway (22%) and Estonia (19%), with smaller shares from Finland (7%), Denmark (6%), and Lithuania (2%). The mean values can be used by building designers and environmental consultants as generic climate data to support early-stage sustainable building design and to address data gaps where product-specific information is unavailable.

papers.title: Iontronic triboelectric tele-perception enabled by ion-relaxation engineering and a lightweight 1D-CNN decoder
papers.authors: Jiaxin Guo, Yan Du, Zhong Lin Wang, Di Wei
papers.abstract: Robots must recognize what is approaching before they touch it. Triboelectric tele-perception meets this need, but its responses stay pinned to the material permittivity (dielectric constant) of the target: the voltage waveform collapses to a scaled copy of the electrostatic coupling, and material identity must then be recovered from a handful of amplitudes. We show that ionic relaxation in an iontronic dielectric breaks this constraint. Dispersing room temperature ionic liquid of BMIMTFSI (10 wt%) in thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) gives an iontronic triboelectric sensor (ITS) whose mobile ions relax on the time scale of an approach event, so that ionic polarization and electrostatic induction act as two independent contributions to the same voltage transient. The resulting waveforms differ in shape, not merely in height: the iontronic film retains 91.57% of its initial output after 10⁵ cycles and resolves four target materials as distinct polarity-amplitude classes at 70 mm. Because the discriminating information lies in the waveform morphology, a generic one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) fed with raw voltage traces classifies the four materials at 90.5% mean accuracy without hand-crafted features. We use this output to drive material-specific robot motions and a polarity-gated three-level warning display. Ionic relaxation thus supplies a design degree of freedom that is orthogonal to permittivity, and it turns an electrostatic proximity signal into a material fingerprint that a small decoder can read.

papers.title: INTELLIGENT AUTOMATED CONTROL SYSTEMS FOR INDUSTRIAL ROBOTS
papers.authors: Nataliia Huliіeva, Borys Prydalnyi, Людмила Михайлівна Самчук, Viktor Sychuk, Yevhenii Myronchuk
papers.abstract: This paper examines the application of machine learning in industrial robot control systems. End-to-end learning, imitation learning, and residual learning are compared through a review of the scientific literature. papers.title: Hybrid robotic-assisted versus laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy for obesity: a 1-year comparative study of perioperative outcomes, weight loss, and obesity-related comorbidities
papers.authors: Yusujiang Tusuntuoheti, Maimaitiaili Maimaitiming, Qiming Huang, Jiaxin Wen, Jing Wu, Kelimu Abudureyimu, Aikebaier Aili
papers.abstract: Background Laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG) represents the most commonly performed bariatric surgery worldwide. Robotic-assisted sleeve gastrectomy (RSG) has emerged as an alternative approach to conventional LSG. However, its higher cost and uncertain clinical advantages have limited widespread adoption. At our center, a hybrid RSG technique was adopted. Objective The purpose of this study is to compare perioperative outcomes, hospitalization cost, 1-year weight reduction, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) status, diabetes mellitus and hypertension outcomes between hybrid RSG and LSG in patients with obesity. Methods We retrospectively analyzed 85 patients with obesity who underwent hybrid RSG or LSG between January 2023 and May 2024. Baseline characteristics, operative variables, postoperative complications, hospitalization cost, weight loss indices, GERD status, and diabetes mellitus and hypertension outcomes were evaluated through 1-year follow-up. Results Of the 85 patients included, 22 underwent hybrid RSG and 63 underwent LSG. No statistically significant differences were detected in the baseline characteristics between the two groups. Hybrid RSG was associated with longer operative time than LSG (158.41 ± 25.93 vs. 125.48 ± 28.56 min, P < 0.001) and higher hospitalization cost (62180.78 ± 7237.77 vs. 46693.87 ± 6054.18 CNY, P < 0.001). No statistically significant between-group differences were detected in intraoperative blood loss, postoperative hospital stays, complications, reoperation, and mortality, or weight loss outcomes at 6 or 12 months. At 12 months, GERD remission, de novo GERD, diabetes and hypertension remission also showed no statistically significant differences. Conclusion In this cohort, hybrid RSG and LSG were both safe and effective for the treatment of obesity. However, hybrid RSG was associated with significantly longer operative time and higher hospitalization cost. No statistically significant between-group differences were detected in 1-year weight loss and obesity-related comorbidity outcomes. Further studies incorporating adjusted analyses, longer follow-up, and comprehensive cost-effectiveness evaluation are needed.

papers.title: Heterogeneous multi agent shared control with reinforcement learning based authority arbitration for semi closed loop EEG based shared autonomy
papers.authors: Ao Zhang
papers.abstract: EEG-based shared autonomy integrates neural commands with autonomous assistance to improve control reliability under uncertain brain signals. However, EEG commands may exhibit varying confidence levels and conflict with autonomous actions, making dynamic authority allocation a key challenge. This study proposes a conflict-aware, functionally heterogeneous multi-agent shared-control framework with reinforcement-learning-based authority arbitration for semi-closed-loop EEG-based shared autonomy. Rather than jointly training all agents through reinforcement learning, the framework uses a pretrained EEG intention agent, a fixed autonomous control agent, and a reinforcement-learning-based authority-arbitration agent with distinct information sources and decision roles. The EEG intention agent outputs the estimated user action and its confidence score, while the autonomous control agent generates an environment-aware assistive action. The authority-arbitration agent then learns the control mode and user-authority ratio from EEG confidence, action disagreement, task state, and a shared task reward. A feedback-guided mechanism further adjusts subsequent authority allocation according to completed task-state transitions. The method was evaluated on the Kaya MI-BCI Dataset and Mobile BCI Dataset using recorded EEG data in a semi-closed-loop virtual-navigation environment rather than real-time human–BCI interaction. It achieved TSR/CRR values of 91.7%/88.4% and 87.8%/84.5%, respectively. Compared with EEG-TD3 Multi-agent Copilot, the method improved TSR by 1.1 and 1.3% points and CRR by 1.5 and 1.8% points on the two datasets, respectively. It also exceeded the matched single-agent RL arbitration baseline in both TSR and CRR. Feature-space, feature-importance, failure-case, and ablation analyses further examined the roles of EEG confidence, action disagreement, functional decomposition, and feedback-guided adjustment. The results support the feasibility of adaptive authority arbitration within the evaluated semi-closed-loop protocol and provide preliminary evidence for subsequent online closed-loop validation.

papers.title: HandPad: A Bimanual Hand Interface for Fluid Window Interactions in VR

papers.title: From a single demonstration to a general policy for contact-rich manipulation

papers.abstract: We present a four-stage Learning from Demonstration (LfD) pipeline that incrementally constructs a general policy for multi-stage contact-rich manipulation from a single human demonstration. papers.title: FlexiCAVE: A Dynamically Configurable High-Resolution Display Facility
papers.authors: Zainab Aamir, Saeed Boorboor, Ahamed Shoaib, Arie E. Kaufman
papers.abstract: Large high-resolution displays (LHRDs) are increasingly central to visualization and visual analytics, offering expansive visual space, simultaneous support for context and detail, and intuitive physical navigation. While advances in resolution and form factor have broadened their use, a persistent challenge remains: most LHRDs adopt static geometries, and even reconfigurable systems typically treat layout adjustment as a setup mechanism rather than as an interaction technique during active analysis. To address this, we introduce the FlexiCAVE, a dynamically reconfigurable LHRD environment featuring rotatable display columns that enable real-time adjustment of horizontal curvature. The system comprises forty high-pixel-density panels arranged across ten columns, providing active stereo visualization at approximately 83 million pixels. Each column rotates inward up to 90°, allowing the display to transform between flat and highly curved layouts during active use. A custom rendering engine synchronizes view perspectives with physical reconfiguration in real time. Through controlled studies and expert evaluations centered on 3D navigation, we found that dynamic reconfiguration reduced spatial judgment error by 51% compared to static flat layouts and by 26% compared to static curved layouts. It also enhanced users’ sense of direction, with participants reporting that the physical display structure provided directional anchoring absent in static systems. We further explored PIVoT (Physical Interaction to Virtual Transformation), mapping physical display rotation to visualization updates. Our findings reveal that physical reconfiguration is most effective when display geometry provides spatially meaningful correspondence to data operations. We derive design principles for reconfigurable display environments and discuss implications for next-generation large-scale visualization systems.

papers.title: EfficientDexGrasp: Diverse and Physically Feasible Dexterous Grasping via Few-Step Diffusion Distillation
papers.authors: Hanyu Huang, Geying Chen, Wen Zhao
papers.abstract: Diffusion models dominate dexterous grasp generation, but their iterative sampling is too slow for latency-sensitive deployment. Distilling a multi-step diffusion teacher into a few-step student exposes two coupled failure modes: distinct grasp modes collapse into a single averaged pose that corresponds to no valid grasp, and the physical refinement the teacher performs at every denoising step is lost, so many student predictions drift into penetration or self-collision. We propose EfficientDexGrasp, a physics-guided distillation framework that addresses both. Contrastive energy distillation shapes an auxiliary energy landscape in which distinct grasp modes remain separate low-energy basins. Gated physics-guided consistency trajectory distillation scales correction with how much worse the student is than the teacher, so predictions at or beyond the teacher’s level receive progressively less. The two modules reinforce each other: correction stays on genuinely degraded predictions and leaves the multimodal structure intact. On DexGraspNet, MultiDex, RealDex, and DexGRAB, EfficientDexGrasp achieves 11×to 69× inference speedups and surpasses the strongest prior baselines by 3.8 to 5.8 points on the stringent Suc.6 metric in the 8-step setting. We further demonstrate deployability on a real robot.

papers.title: Driving Intelligence: The Amber Book
papers.authors: Gabriel Seiberth, J. Mark Bishop
papers.abstract: Driving Intelligence examines artificial intelligence through the lens of autonomous driving, using driving as a real-world test case for intelligence. At a time when expectations of artificial general intelligence are rising, the book challenges how intelligence is defined and measured, arguing that current benchmarks saturate, leak, and can be gamed. The book develops a framework for understanding intelligence through the concept of real-world agency, with autonomous driving as its central case study. It argues that driving uniquely combines scale, open-ended environmental complexity, and continuous multi-agent interaction under uncertainty. Unlike most AI benchmarks, which are static or isolated, autonomous driving unfolds in a dynamic physical and social world that cannot be exhaustively specified in advance. The book analyzes failure modes in perception, prediction, planning, and interaction, showing how these limitations reveal a deeper gap between statistical learning from large-scale data and genuine agency. This volume, Amber, benchmarks today's autonomous driving systems against real-world performance data and tracks the shift from language-based AI toward Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems in robotics. The book's central contribution is to reframe autonomous driving as a benchmark for intelligence grounded in real-world agency. It identifies systematic limitations in current AI approaches and clarifies what is missing for genuine autonomy, providing a concrete framework for evaluating progress in Real-World AI and Physical AI. The book will be essential reading for professionals, academics, and students working and researching AI and autonomous vehicles, as well as the interested general reader.

papers.title: Augmenting Data Physicalization Using Visuo-Tactile Illusions
papers.authors: Xiaojiao Du, Kadek Ananta Satriadi, Adam Drogemuller, James A. Walsh, Ross Smith, Andrew Cunningham
papers.abstract: Data physicalizations fabricated by 3D printers are limited in their ability to dynamically vary their form and tactile properties without refabrication, thereby hindering reusability. In particular, tactile properties on the surface of a physicalization (i.e., surface roughness ) cannot be dynamically adjusted as the data change. To address this limitation, we explore a novel method to increase the reusability of a data physicalization, namely perceived tactile modulation (PTM). Our method enables the perception of varying surface roughness levels on a static data physicalization through the use of virtual reality. By altering the visual roughness of the virtual model, we modulate the user’s perception of tactile roughness, thereby influencing how the physicalization is interpreted through touch and expanding the range of ordinal data values that can be encoded. We conducted two studies to design and evaluate this method. In the first study (N = 20), Just Noticeable Differences (JNDs) were established for perceivable visuo-tactile channels in virtual reality environments. The second study (N = 12) investigates the application of our method across two levels of interactive representation: static and interactive. Our findings show that PTM can reliably modulate perceived roughness in static physicalization, while its effectiveness for supporting dynamic, single-artifact updates (interactive encoding) requires further investigation. We present a series of recommendations for applying PTM techniques in data physicalization.

papers.abstract: Modern children are growing up in a digital world that offers immense potential, with many beginning to use technology from an early age. This digital environment presents countless opportunities for learning and development, but it also necessitates a balanced, thoughtful approach to raising children as informed, open-minded citizens. Industry 4.0, driven by artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, and the Internet of Things (IoT), is reshaping how children think, learn, and interact with the world. The integration of AI into children's lives is a complex issue, bringing both significant benefits and notable risks. On the positive side, AI can power educational tools, interactive games, and personalized learning experiences, fostering cognitive development and creativity. However, it also introduces serious concerns, such as exposure to cyber threats, potential manipulation, privacy violations through data collection, and increased access to harmful content. This study explores the dual impact of information technologies on children's digital development. By analyzing these multifaceted dynamics, the research aims to offer recommendations for maximizing the advantages of the digital age while ensuring a safer and more supportive online environment for children.

papers.title: What One Sample Cannot See: Why Fewer Denoising Steps Can Score Higher on Physics Benchmarks
papers.authors: Yutao Li, Chen Wang
papers.abstract: When a storm can head north or south, a forecast down the middle may score better under squared error than either plausible path. The same paradox appears when video generators are tested as world models: fewer denoising steps can raise physics scores even as videos blur or stop moving early. Why? Physics-IQ compares each generated video with one recording, although a scene can have multiple valid futures. An exact decomposition shows its scores can reward reduced variation among generated futures, even when their distribution becomes less accurate. We introduce Kernel Physics-IQ to remove this incentive in expectation, needing only two independent samples per condition. Two-step sampling lowers Kernel Physics-IQ in all five image-to-video models. For CogVideoX, the official score rises by 0.055 while ours falls by 0.131. Changing the sampling schedule reveals further differences official scores miss. In controlled physical systems with known outcome probabilities, our metric favors the true distribution over collapsed predictions. In short, a world model should be judged not only by how closely one video matches what happened, but by how faithfully its predictions represent what could have happened.

papers.title: WAMotor: Accelerating World Action Models via Speculative Inference under Dual Nonuniform Denoising Dynamics
papers.authors: Zexun Lin, Yuan Feng, Xike Xie
papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) unify world modeling and action generation for robotic control by integrating flow-matching velocities, yet suffer from high multi-step denoising latency. Recent studies have explored speculative inference to accelerate WAMs by drafting and verifying denoising steps in parallel. However, existing methods either require training task-specific draft models or overlook critical WAM denoising dynamics when reusing past velocities as drafts. We revisit the denoising dynamics of WAMs and identify a dual nonuniformity that breaks standard velocity-reuse assumptions: velocity smoothness is nonuniform as adjacent velocity residuals differ sharply at early and final steps, so reuse there yields large residuals, which nonuniform integration time steps further translate into local state errors that accumulate into the final action distribution. Accordingly, we formalize this by theoretically deriving a trajectory error tolerance bound that characterizes how velocity residuals and integration time steps affect the final action distribution. Based on this, we propose WAMotor, the first speculative inference method tailored to the dual nonuniformity in WAMs. It selects reliable anchor velocities by deferring speculation and employs time-step-aware verification that scales acceptance thresholds by integration time step size. WAMotor offers plug-and-play benefits, enabling seamless integration with prior WAMs. Extensive evaluations on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and LIBERO-Plus show that WAMotor achieves 2.86$\times$--4.28$\times$ end-to-end speedups while maintaining task success rates. papers.title: UniVEP: Unifying Velocity and Endpoint Prediction for Robot Manipulation

Inspired by these findings, we introduce UniVEP, which learns both prediction targets together with consistency supervision and switches from endpoint recovery to velocity refinement as noise drops. On RoboTwin, UniVEP hits 61.36% success with one StarVLA run, beating the best single-target baseline at sixteen runs (59.96%). papers.title: Trajectory-Calibrated Merging of Embodied Policies
papers.authors: Wenshuo Chen, Honglei Jin, Le Yang, Jianfei Song, Shaofeng Liang, Lei Wang, Junze Zhu, Kailong Wang, et al.
papers.abstract: Robot foundation models are increasingly adapted into task specialists to expand their embodied capabilities. Yet these capabilities remain fragmented across separate policies, and existing model-merging methods do not reliably preserve them during closed-loop execution: parameter-space alignment provides only an indirect proxy for behavior, while regression may fail to preserve behavior at states not covered by its calibration inputs. We present Trajectory-Calibrated Regression (TCR), an execution-aware, gradient-free framework that consolidates robot specialists into a single policy. Across two complementary timescales, TCR collects calibration inputs from expert rollouts spanning different stages of task execution and from intermediate states within iterative action generation. To account for representation shifts introduced by merging, TCR recomputes each block's input through the already merged blocks. It then uses each expert's computation within the block to form module inputs and fits merged weights to match the experts' linear outputs. A two-pass calibration procedure further refines the merged policy using separate rollout caches while retaining the frozen specialists as teachers. The resulting model preserves the original inference graph and requires neither expert routing nor additional gradient training. On LIBERO, TCR merges four $π_{0.5}$ specialists and achieves 77.83% success across 1,200 evaluation episodes, outperforming FeatCal, RegMean, and direct weight averaging by 9.50, 24.17, and 33.00 percentage points, respectively.

This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. papers.abstract: The accelerated use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing the financial services industry and the banking sector in terms of improving the efficiency of their operations, customer experience, risk management and the effectiveness of strategic decision-making. The proposed researc examines the profound influence of artificial intelligence (AI) on the financial sector, analyzing its many effects on operations, risk management and client experiences. By examining the incorporation of machine learning algorithms, natural language processing and robotic process automation, the substantial improvements in efficiency and reductions in costs that Artificial Intelligence (AI) provides to financial institutions was revealed. Moreover, the study explores the consequences of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in improving fraud detection procedures and reducing operational risks, thereby strengthening the sector's ability to withstand challenges. Nevertheless, the study also acknowledges the risks related to data privacy, ethical considerations and the possibility of employment displacement, emphasizing the necessity for strong regulatory frameworks.

papers.title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely
papers.authors: Zheyuan Liu, Chuhan Wang, Jinduo Guo, Yue Huang, Xiangchi Yuan, Ningshan Ma, Meng Jiang
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot's other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3\%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.

papers.title: TacInno: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models the Contact Dynamics Beyond Vision and Action
papers.authors: Weile Li, Yunfan Lou, Muqing Shi, Zihao Zhang, Zhenbiao Huang, Boxian Yao, Xiyu Zhu, Zhibo Pang
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently been equipped with tactile sensing to perceive visually subtle contact events in contact-rich manipulation. However, adding tactile input yields inconsistent gains, and some visuo-tactile VLA models rely little on tactile input, because much of the tactile change, such as the gel deformation during gripper closure, is predictable from visual observations and executed actions. To address this problem, we introduce TacInno, which isolates the contact dynamics that vision and executed actions cannot explain, termed tactile innovation, and uses tactile innovation only as a training target. Specifically, the TacInno tokenizer, conditioned on visual observations and executed actions, compresses the future tactile change into a discrete code, and the policy, TacInno-VLA, learns to predict the code, adding no module for the code at deployment. TacInno-VLA achieves average success rates of 87.5% across six simulation tasks and 70.5% across four real-world tasks, outperforming the strongest visuo-tactile baseline by 10.7 and 9.0 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies validate the contributions of visual and action conditioning, multi-frame encoding, and auxiliary code prediction. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile innovation as a supervision signal for contact-rich manipulation.

papers.title: StreamEgo: Streaming Exocentric-to-Egocentric Video Generation
papers.authors: Tianyi Xu, Boyang Lyu, Yunkai Tang, Kairan Ding, Jiahang Li, Weiyu Guo, Yandong Guo, Shuchen Weng, et al.
papers.abstract: Exocentric-to-egocentric (Exo2Ego) video generation transforms third-person recordings into first-person viewpoints, unlocking immersive AR/VR experiences and scalable demonstration synthesis for embodied robotics. Extending it to a streaming setting is expected to further enable live applications. However, existing methods suffer from degraded manipulation regions, overfitting and confinement to fixed-length clips with prohibitive latency. To address these limitations, we present StreamEgo, a real-time framework for unbounded, generalizable Exo2Ego video generation. To resolve intricate manipulation dynamics while supporting the streaming pipeline, a streaming dual-branch prior provides pixel-aligned guidance for translating appearance and skeletal kinematics. We also introduce a region-aware loss curriculum to improve generalization and stabilize multi-objective diffusion training. Furthermore, we distill the model into a chunk-wise autoregressive model, augmented with a region-aware corruption mechanism and a first-chunk curriculum, enabling high-quality, generalizable real-time streaming Exo2Ego generation at 24.3 FPS on a single H100 GPU.

papers.title: SteerTrace: Tracing How Target Attacks Steer World Action Models
papers.authors: Yukun Dai, Tianshi Wang, Fengling Li, Jingjing Li, Xin Li, Lei Zhu
papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) predict future videos and actions with one backbone, and their imagined future is often seen as a safety signal. We introduce SteerTrace, a targeted universal attack on WAMs that also traces its effect inside the model. One $\ell_\infty$-bounded (4/255) perturbation per model, shared across frames, tasks, and camera views, pushes the executed action toward an attacker-chosen target. On eight WAMs from four families (FastWAM, Faster-WAM, OpenWAM and LingBot-VA) on LIBERO and RoboTwin, it drives task success close to zero and moves the attacked action toward the target. Same-budget noise and BadWAM produce little action shift in the target direction. We use the signed targeted effect to measure how much of the effect each intervention removes or reproduces. Under the standard attack, restoring future tokens removes 61-94% of the targeted effect in the five models whose action experts attend to them. When the attack is constrained to keep the predicted future close to the clean prediction, the targeted effect can become more dependent on current-frame tokens. In three of these five models, restoring current-frame tokens removes 87-99% of the effect, compared with 9-15% for future tokens. In six models, restoring just 0.36% of the FFN neurons in layers 10-29 of the video expert removes 72-96% of the targeted effect. Residual directions 2-16 hold only 11-18% of the shift energy, yet removing them cancels most of the targeted effect.

papers.title: Spatially Conditioned Trajectory Diffusion
papers.authors: Yefim Nudelman, Dor Atzmon, Tom Tirer
papers.abstract: Multi-Robot Motion Planning (MRMP) requires trajectories that avoid environmental obstacles and collisions between robots in a shared workspace. Diffusion-based planners often address obstacle avoidance through sampling-time guidance, while some conditioned approaches aggregate map geometry into a global representation. We present Spatially Conditioned Trajectory Diffusion (SCTD), a map-conditioned trajectory generator for multi-robot planning. SCTD retains multiple position-aware occupancy tokens accessed through cross-attention throughout a temporal U-Net, with hard endpoint inpainting enforcing start and goal states. One model trained on single-robot demonstrations across procedural environments generates obstacle-aware trajectories without sampling-time obstacle-cost guidance. High-level Conflict-Based Search (CBS) coordinates these trajectories through constrained replanning, retaining inter-agent guidance during sampling and reusing the model across workspace layouts and team sizes. Experiments assess single-robot success and trajectory quality, generalization to unfamiliar layouts with added obstacles, and coordinated multi-robot planning. On 15,000 held-out tasks, SCTD achieves higher success than the evaluated guided diffusion baseline, with the largest gains on hard-detour tasks, while trajectory-quality comparisons show smoother trajectories. Conditioning ablations show higher success with spatial tokens than with a global map embedding, and map-replacement tests demonstrate dependence on the supplied geometry. The resulting multi-robot system achieves higher team success than the compared diffusion baselines, with experiments covering teams of up to 15 robots.

papers.title: Safety-Critical Control with Lyapunov and Barrier Functions: From Smooth to Nonsmooth Methods
papers.authors: Jianglin Lan
papers.abstract: This book presents a comprehensive framework for designing control systems that must operate safely in complex, real-world environments. It addresses the critical challenge facing modern autonomous systems: how to guarantee both stability and safety when dynamics are inherently nonsmooth. Safety-Critical Control with Lyapunov and Barrier Functions: From Smooth to Nonsmooth Methods presents a unified methodology integrating stability (via Lyapunov functions) and safety constraint enforcement (via barrier functions). Its key strength is the rigorous treatment of nonsmooth dynamics using generalized derivatives, set-valued mappings, and differential inclusions. The text progresses systematically from nonsmooth analysis and stability theory through safety enforcement and unified synthesis methods, including optimization-based quadratic program controllers and Lyapunov-barrier function designs. It bridges abstract theory with real-time implementation, addressing practical constraints such as input saturation and dynamic environments. Readers gain theoretical understanding and practical tools to design control systems for autonomous vehicles, robotics, energy networks, and other safety-critical applications requiring simultaneous performance and constraint satisfaction. This book is designed for graduate students, researchers, and practitioners in control systems engineering, robotics, autonomous systems, and applied mathematics who require advanced methods for safety-critical applications. It is particularly valuable for those working on autonomous vehicles, robotic manipulation, cyber-physical systems, and other domains where safety constraints cannot be compromised.

papers.title: SCCV-6D: Sparse Canonical Coordinate Voting for Holistic Multi-View RGB-D 6D Pose Estimation in Robotic Bin Picking
papers.authors: Nico Leuze, Samed Dogan, Maximilian Hoh, Henry Schaub, Alfred Schöttl
papers.abstract: Industrial bin picking requires pose estimates that are accurate under clutter, partial occlusion, and the reflective, texture-less nature of manufactured parts. Most recent approaches to 6D pose estimation follow multi-stage pipelines. These achieve high accuracy, but incur memory and runtime footprints that do not cope with the operational constraints of many real-world industrial deployments. Holistic pipelines estimate poses in a single pass, with cost controlled through indiscriminate subsampling or lowered resolution. Continuing this line, we present SCCV-6D, a fully sparse multi-view RGB-D estimator. We reconstruct the 3D space at millimeter precision, prune background via a staged heatmap mechanism, and predict class, translation offset and rotation at highest resolution for an arbitrary number of objects simultaneously. Rotation is formulated as canonical coordinate voting. Points vote for their canonical object coordinates with an associated confidence, enabling closed-form pose recovery with a symmetry-aware weighted Procrustes solve. Along an in-cluster point recovery induced by offset votes, this removes time-consuming post-processing stages. We reuse the task-supervised attention priors from the heatmap formulation for a novel attention-gated distillation objective that reweights teacher-student feature alignment. On the IPD test split we report competitive 0.826 AP at 1.13 s per scene, significantly faster than the leading entries. On MV-YCB our approach reaches 96.1 ADD-S, and remains competitive even on the densely packed bins of ROBI.

papers.title: Risk-Controlled Test-Time Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Zixuan Liu, Hashem Haghbayan, Zizhan Zheng, Siavash Khajavi
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) models enable efficient test-time adaptation by leveraging expert demonstrations as additional context without updating model parameters. However, even when retrieved demonstrations are relevant to the current task, the VLA may fail to effectively utilize the retrieved information, ultimately leading to task failure. To address this challenge, we propose R2-VLA, a risk-controlled retrieval-augmented VLA framework that enables reliable test-time adaptation by satisfying a user-specified task success rate requirement with minimal expert assistance. Specifically, R2-VLA learns an uncertainty predictor that estimates the uncertainty of the VLA's predicted actions given the retrieved demonstrations, guiding when to act autonomously or request expert assistance. We further introduce a task-level risk-control procedure that calibrates the uncertainty threshold to satisfy a user-specified task-failure risk requirement. Moreover, R2-VLA continually incorporates expert corrections into its retrieval memory to improve future adaptation while preserving the prescribed task-level risk guarantee. Experiments across three VLA backbones and four LIBERO benchmark suites demonstrate that R2-VLA improves average task success by 9.2--11.2 percentage points, achieving the desired target with fewer expert requests. These results highlight the effectiveness of connecting the usefulness of retrieved demonstrations with task-level risk control to enable successful robotic manipulation.

papers.title: RefreshGrad: An Online Adaptive Data-sampling Method for Diffusion-based Visuomotor Learning
papers.authors: Dijia Zhan, Jinyi Li, Xuemiao Xu, Yan Zhou, Yu Liu, Shaoshan Liu, Jie Tang
papers.abstract: Training vision-language-action (VLA) policies from demonstrations typically samples trajectory segments uniformly or relies on static offline data curation before training. However, we find that demonstration data vary sharply in supervision value across temporal windows, and that each window's value to the policy evolves substantially during training rather than being fixed or captured by raw loss alone. Motivated by this finding, we propose RefreshGrad, an online adaptive data-sampling framework that periodically scores temporal windows from the evolving policy using five policy-native signals and dynamically adjusts their sampling weights during training. RefreshGrad focuses optimization on informative, learnable windows without altering the policy architecture, training objective, or inference cost. Across ten LIBERO-Plus manipulation tasks, RefreshGrad boosts average success from 60.7% (Uniform) and 68.2% (FAKTUAL) to 76.1% under visual perturbations, and from 57.4% and 73.3% to 81.3% in clean scenes.

papers.title: Reference-Twist-Based Velocity-Domain Spatiotemporal Calibration for mmWave Radar, Event Camera, and IMU
papers.authors: Zhenghao Zou, Yang Lyu, Xiaohu Guo, Chunhui Zhao, Quan Pan
papers.abstract: Multi-sensor navigation requires a common spatial and temporal basis, but geometric calibration relies on targets, features, point clouds, or pose associations that are difficult to establish across mmWave radars, event cameras, and inertial measurement units (IMUs). These sensors nevertheless share rigid-body motion. This paper formulates reference-conditioned velocity-domain spatiotemporal calibration for a rigid suite of two mmWave radars, one event camera, and two IMUs. Given a trusted reference body twist, radar Doppler, event normal flow, and inertial measurements are regressed against the same motion to estimate relative rotations, lever arms, time offsets, and sensor-specific bias and scale without artificial targets, structure from motion, or cross-modal point-cloud registration. The reference is treated as a conditioning input rather than a sensor to be calibrated. We compare joint and reference- conditioned estimation, derive conditional identifiability and CRLB-level covariance and bias bounds, and state the operating conditions under which conditioning is informative. Indoor and forest recordings with axis-separated motion evaluate initial- ization, temporal alignment, motion degeneracy, reference-input sensitivity, and residual consistency. Because the reference does not add physical observability, the estimates remain conditional on reference accuracy, synchronization, motion excitation, and projection diversity.

papers.title: Reference-Free Humanoid Skateboarding via Termination-Shaped Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Ganeshvar Soenessardien, Michael Przystupa, Kevin Sebastian Luck
papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion research has advanced rapidly on walking and running, but \emph {object-mediated} locomotion, in which a robot must coordinate its body with a passive external object, remains difficult. One challenging task is skateboarding, which requires simultaneous interaction with the ground and a passive but movable platform to achieve forward motion. Current methods for tackling skateboarding with humanoid robots either require human demonstrations or utilise analytic steering models that require system identification. In this paper, we introduce a deep reinforcement learning framework that does not rely on prior data such as demonstrations and enables robots such as the K1 humanoid to learn to skateboard using model-free learning. The method combines task rewards with exploit-blocking terminations. We introduce a number of constraints restricting behaviours such as losing the planted board foot, standing with both feet on the board, excessive twisting, separation from the board, and unstable board motion. Their changing prevalence during training produces an implicit progression from stance control towards sustained robot--board locomotion.

papers.title: Reasoning on Call: Efficient Agentic Robot Control for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Zilang Cen, Chao Tang, Fangcheng Liu, Weishi Mi, Wei Hao, JiaYu Xu, Dehao Huang, Yehui Tang, et al.
papers.abstract: Large multimodal models can support long-horizon robot manipulation, but frequent model calls incur substantial latency and token costs. The central challenge is determining when agent assistance or intervention is needed and whether errors require correcting robot execution, subtask planning, or both. To address this problem, we propose RoC (Reasoning on Call), an efficient framework that coordinates a low-level policy and a high-level reasoning agent through an online task-state monitor. The monitor combines temporal visual observations with ordered interaction memory to jointly estimate progress within the active subtask and predict its successor. These predictions guide event-triggered agent review for coordinated execution repair and plan revision. Verified outcomes govern memory updates and subtask transitions, allowing routine execution to remain with the policy while reasoning focuses on decisions requiring additional assessment. On RMBench, RoC improves task success rate by 24.0 percentage points and reduces token consumption by 65.3% compared with the strongest agent-based baseline. It also outperforms the strongest policy-based baseline by 15.1 percentage points in task success rate. Real-world experiments further validate its effectiveness across three long-horizon manipulation tasks. Overall, RoC supports efficient agent intervention and coordinated recovery across execution and planning for long-horizon robot manipulation.

papers.title: Point Dynamics as Proxy for Robotic World Models
papers.authors: Dong An, Tianyu Liu, Haoran Ding, Wen Yang, Anqing Duan, Zhengzhong Liu, Eric P. Xing, Guangyi Liu
papers.abstract: Robotic world models predict future video frames from the current observation and a sequence of robot actions. While recent models follow the given actions closely, manipulated objects often collapse or move inconsistently with the action. We attribute this to the conditioning: an action, or a rendering of the robot, specifies where the robot goes but not how the scene responds, leaving a single video model to infer the interaction dynamics implicitly while also rendering appearance. We therefore separate dynamics prediction from visual rendering, with 3D point dynamics as the proxy between them. Specifically, we lift the first frame into 3D points, simulate how they respond to the robot's motion with a learned point dynamics model, and render the simulated points back into pixel-aligned videos that any video model can read. In controlled experiments on the DROID dataset with two video renderers of different architectures, this point dynamics proxy reduces object motion error by 8.6% and 6.2% without degrading image quality, and by 8.1% on a real bimanual robot. Moreover, the video follows the simulation: more accurate dynamics yield more accurate object motion, and editing the points steers the video. This suggests that advances in dynamics modeling can translate into more faithful robotic world models.

papers.title: Planning to Stop: Factored Certification and Terminal Repair for Noncircular Robots
papers.authors: Runtian Zheng, Congpeng Zhang, Ying Liu
papers.abstract: Tight-space navigation requires a robot to clear obstacles and stop inside its goal despite uncertainty. We present GeoDiff, a motion-program planner coupling original-goal stopped-set inclusion, witness-guided terminal repair, and factored proof compilation. An exact feasible-translation characterization guides repair; request-local reuse reduces repeated geometric work. We establish conditions for compiler equivalence and reach-and-stop soundness. Across 11,440 floorplan-derived jobs, GeoDiff certifies 61/139 tasks at 5-cm tolerance within 15 s, versus 44/139 for the stop-set baseline. The strongest observed external certificate adapter certifies 13/139 tasks from 119/139 native routes, separating route availability from certification. On tasks derived from public BARN maps, GeoDiff certifies 202/270 at 5-cm tolerance for a Jackal-shaped body, versus 3/270 for the portal baseline. Development analyses distinguish emitter savings from solver coverage, and 1,420 route-tracking episodes characterize the execution interface. These results show how terminal reasoning and proof reuse increase finite-budget certification coverage while preserving the original physical task and goal.

papers.title: PhysVAM: Physics-oriented Future Value Action Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
papers.authors: Yuxiang Yang, Jingbo Zhang, Jiaru Zhong, Junliang Chen, Yirui Zhou, Guangming Wang, Haitao Lin, Huaiyuan Xu, et al.
papers.abstract: Predicting future scene or object states does not necessarily reveal how robot-object interactions will advance or hinder a task. This challenge is particularly pronounced in dynamic robotic manipulation, where objects continue moving during perception and execution. Effective action generation therefore requires not only modeling object dynamics but also anticipating how future interactions will shape task progress. To this end, we propose \textbf{PhysVAM}, a Physics-oriented Future Value Action Model that represents anticipated interactions through their effects on future task progress. This value-based formulation provides task-directed foresight without reconstructing future visual states. Conditioned on current observations and historical object and robot motion, PhysVAM jointly learns action generation and multi-horizon future-value prediction. The value branch learns horizon-specific latent representations through future task-value prediction from successful and failed trajectories. These future-value representations are integrated into the action policy through gated cross-attention, guiding action generation toward interactions that facilitate task success. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate superior task success, with absolute success-rate improvements of 27.0 and 27.5 percentage points over the strongest baselines in simulation and real-world tasks, respectively. papers.title: PhyDEX: A Benchmark for Physical Reasoning in Vision-Language-Action Models via Dynamic Extrinsic Dexterity
papers.authors: Hao Vo, Taisei Hanyu, Yuki Ikebe, Pham Tri Quang, Sreevenkata Anjani Tishita Godavarthi, Nghi D. Q. Bui, Daniel Sonntag, Chase Rainwater, et al.
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly in language-conditioned robotic manipulation, yet existing benchmarks mainly evaluate gripper--object contact and largely ignore how objects interact with the environment through gravity, friction, inertia, and mass distribution. As a result, it remains unclear whether current policies truly understand physics or merely interpolate from their training data. We address this gap through the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity and introduce PhyDEX, a throwing benchmark in which a robot must infer an object's mass, center of mass, and friction to send it to a destination beyond its kinematic workspace. PhyDEX contains 35K trajectories (143 hours) across nine tasks and 100 scenes, covering uniform, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects with static, multiple, and moving destinations. All data are generated by a scalable, fully automatic pipeline that combines grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop throw optimization under randomized physical properties. We evaluate three representative VLAs, GR00T N1.7, DynamicVLA, and ForceVLA, and find that all achieve success rates below 3\%. Our analysis reveals two key bottlenecks: limited robustness of pretrained models, which causes most failures before the throw, and physical blindness, as providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles success. Experiments on a humanoid robot and in the real world show the same failure patterns. We hope PhyDEX will drive the development of physically grounded robot policies.

papers.title: PUPPET: Physical-Unified Platform for Presence, Embodiment, and Teleoperation
papers.authors: Mahika Vats, Milan Groshev, Carlos Gomez Cubero, Eduardo Castelló Ferrer
papers.abstract: Remote access to robotics hardware does not by itself guarantee usable experimental data. A teleoperated trial can complete the task and still produce an incomplete or inconsistent record. PUPPET aims to solve this problem by presenting a cyber-physical framework that opens a physical robotics laboratory through a continuously synchronized VR replica of the robot, stranding environment, and task objects. In addition, PUPPET integrates a trial validation pipeline built into the experimental workflow. We evaluated PUPPET in a within-subject study with 30 participants, who performed the same table-to-shelf object-transfer task in person, through 2D teleoperation, and through PUPPET. VR reduced post-learning completion time by 27.7% over 2D (68.7,s vs. 95.0,s), statistically indistinguishable from in-person execution (72.1,s). It also produced more validation-ready (85.6% vs. 66.0%) and intervention-free (89.7% vs. 67.2%) trials. With PUPPET we show that modality shapes the remote task performance and the reusability of the resulting experimental record.
