papers.title: Where Do Human-to-Robot Transfer Gains Come From?
papers.authors: Jiachen Li, Shihao Li, Soovadeep Bakshi, Longteng Fan, Dongmei Chen, Long Chen, Zhuo Xu
papers.abstract: Human data can support robot policy pretraining, but gains attributed to a data recipe may also reflect subset size, training variability, or downstream adaptation. In an HPT implementation on a 20-task MetaWorld suite with three training blocks, a constrained random 5,000-recording subset matches most of the task-informed subset's gain over the 40,000-recording pool at 20,000 updates (3.69 of 4.29 percentage points), leaving equal-size selection differences of 0.60 points at 5,000 recordings and 0.45 points at 1,250 recordings, with wide paired intervals. Across 12 comparisons, task orderings repeat across seeds for several contrasts, but a fixed predictor built from the other two seeds trails the mean or difficulty reference in at least one held-out fold for every comparison. Neither mechanism probe shows its predicted positive interaction: task-slot mismatch yields an interaction of $-0.0347$ points after adaptation, and in a six-task observation experiment the observation-by-pretraining interaction changes sign between seeds ($-18.29$ and $+1.04$ points) while full-state pretraining gains are positive in both ($+6.37$ and $+2.31$ points). This retrospective study shows how equal-size and capacity controls, seed-level reporting, and targeted interventions change the interpretation of apparent transfer gains.

papers.title: When the World Is the Test Suite: Agentic Intelligence for the Physical World
papers.authors: Kaixin Li, Meng Luo, Yanlin Li, Yuchen Tian, Xiang Liu, Xiangru Jian, Yan Yang, Zhiheng Xi, et al.
papers.abstract: Coding agents built to repair software now write, test, and repair programs for robots, laboratories, and industrial controllers. Unlike in software engineering, no test suite comes with the code. Whether a program works must be established by running it on a robot, in a physics simulator, or through the policies it helps to train, and such evidence is costly to obtain and can itself be wrong. As these agents take on more physical tasks, how their programs are judged matters as much as how they are written. This paper examines this emerging area, agentic intelligence for the physical world, by treating the world as the program's test suite. We organize the discussion around three questions: how agents write programs for the physical world, how these programs are tested, and how agents learn from the results. We first trace how language models for robots and software engineering agents came together, ask which software testing practices carry over to physical tests, and describe each program by where it sits relative to the actuator and by what judges it. For writing, we cover programs that act as robot policies and programs that support policy learning by producing rewards, tasks, and training worlds. For testing, we examine what physical trials cost, what traces, learned judges, simulators, and formal checks can establish in their place, and what safety requires beyond task success. For learning, we discuss how tested programs are retained as experience, in skill libraries and in model weights. Finally, we turn to benchmarks and evaluation practice and outline open challenges. Writing programs is becoming cheap, while trustworthy evidence about what they do remains costly. Progress will therefore depend on a physical counterpart of continuous integration: verification cheap enough to run often, reliable enough to trust under search, and maintained alongside the experience it validates.

papers.title: Warehouse Mobile Manipulation with Large Language Models and Foundation Models
papers.authors: Zhaoqi Chen
papers.abstract: Mobile manipulators can move between storage locations and handle goods, but transferring the semantic capabilities of foundation models to dependable warehouse operations remains constrained by execution interfaces, data coverage, and operating conditions. This thematic critical review examines perception, reasoning, planning and execution, and data and generalization. It compares hierarchical approaches with vision-language-action models and assesses their relevance to warehouse tasks using representative studies. Its distinctive value lies in relating model interfaces and transfer limits to warehouse order fulfillment, where stock-keeping unit (SKU) verification, shelf access, and onboard resource limits must be considered together. The evidence indicates that foundation models reorganize selected interfaces between observations, task descriptions, and actions; they do not remove the need for geometric feasibility checks, low-level control, or failure recovery. Open-vocabulary recognition must be connected to item-level verification, while semantic generalization should be distinguished from the acquisition of new motor skills. Reported transfer gains also depend on the task, embodiment, and adaptation budget. The review identifies order completion, coordinated base-arm motion, and measurable adaptation costs as priorities for research and evaluation. These conclusions support method selection and experimental design rather than a claim of validated warehouse deployment.

papers.title: VoxelSBFL: Voxel-Level Spectrum-Based Failure Prediction for Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Arusa Kanwal, Pablo Valle, Paola Roggero, Miren Illarramendi, Shaukat Ali, Aitor Arrieta
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action generation to control robots. Testing these systems produces trajectories and task outcomes, but existing approaches provide limited guidance on using these recorded trajectories to assess subsequent executions or inform policy repair. We conjecture that, for a given policy and task, traversing certain workspace regions is associated with a higher likelihood of failure. To investigate this conjecture, we propose VoxelSBFL, a black-box adaptation of Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) in which workspace voxels replace program elements as units of analysis. Recorded tool-center-point (TCP) trajectories provide binary voxel coverage, which is combined with execution outcomes to construct suspiciousness maps using established SBFL formulas. These maps identify failure-associated regions and score unseen trajectories without requiring internal model access. We evaluate 34 spectrum-based techniques across four VLA models using 96,000 Pick-Up trajectories in simulation and compare the leading techniques against eight action- and trajectory-based metrics. VoxelSBFL obtains an overall macro ROC-AUC of 0.704, significantly outperforming state-of-the art baselines. Sensitivity analyses show that performance varies with spatial granularity and training-set size. These findings support spatial spectra for VLA execution assessment and motivate future research on runtime monitoring, self-healing and targeted policy improvement.

papers.title: VSpark: Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.authors: Suho Yoo, Youngjoon Jang, Hyebin Cho, Taeyeop Lee, Jaewook Jeong, Joon Son Chung
papers.abstract: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in a single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and a draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to a wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLA's hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping the VLA's decoding lossless.

papers.title: VLM-guided Grounding Expert for Generalised Referring Expression Comprehension
papers.authors: Mingcheng Zhu, Wentian Xu, Tao Lin, Shiying Duan, Ziyun Liang, Xuecheng Qi, Junyang Chen, Kuo Li, et al.
papers.abstract: Generalised referring expression comprehension (GREC) aims to identify and localise the zero, one or multiple objects referred to by a language expression. In robotic manipulation, grounding also needs to remain accurate when requests for the same objects are paraphrased or embedded in additional context in robotics. However, grounding expert models are sensitive to instruction variation, while generative vision--language models (VLMs) struggle with complete target recovery and rejection of absent targets. These complementary limitations motivate combining the contextual representations of VLMs with the direct spatial prediction capabilities of grounding experts. We therefore introduce VLM-guided Grounding Expert (VGE), which combines a frozen VLM with a trainable grounding expert through layerwise joint attention and text-conditioned instance scoring. These interfaces leverage multimodal understanding of the VLM to guide object-query refinement and candidate selection while retaining direct bounding-box prediction. Across three datasets, VGE achieves the highest averaged F1 score among the evaluated methods on all five test splits, with differences of at most 1.2 percentage points across instruction conditions within each split. On the dataset with robotic scenes, VGE also achieves the highest F1 across instruction variants and no-target, single-target and multiple-target cases. VGE provides a $5.3$--$13.0\times$ inference speedup over the baseline with the same VLM base model. These results support combining VLM context with specialised spatial prediction to address both grounding challenges, with particularly strong performance in robotic scenes. papers.title: VDAWorld: World Modelling via VLM-Directed Abstraction and Simulation
papers.authors: Felix O'Mahony, Roberto Cipolla, Ayush Tewari
papers.abstract: Generative video models, a leading approach to world modelling, face fundamental limitations. They often violate physical and logical rules, lack interactivity, and operate as opaque black boxes ill-suited for building structured, queryable worlds. To overcome these challenges, we propose a new paradigm focused on distilling an image caption pair into a tractable, abstract representation optimized for simulation. We introduce VDAWorld, a framework where a Vision-Language Model (VLM) acts as an intelligent agent to orchestrate this process. The VLM autonomously constructs a grounded (2D or 3D) scene representation by selecting from a suite of vision tools, and accordingly chooses a compatible physics simulator (e.g., rigid body, fluid) to act upon it. VDAWorld can then infer latent dynamics from the static scene to predict plausible future states. Our experiments show that this combination of intelligent abstraction and adaptive simulation results in a versatile world model capable of producing high quality simulations across a wide range of scenarios. We demonstrate several applications of VDAWorld across interactive control and counterfactual generation, and physical and logical reasoning, achieving state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks.

papers.title: Unifying Physics-Based Humanoid Interaction with a Context-Conditioned Interaction Prior
papers.authors: Jianan Li, Xiao Chen, Tien-Tsin Wong
papers.abstract: Developing unified physics-based humanoid controllers that can navigate complex 3D scenes and manipulate objects remains a longstanding challenge. Existing approaches are often specialized for either locomotion or object-centric manipulation, or rely on task-specific reward engineering that does not scale well across diverse behaviors. We present CHIP, a unified, physics-grounded framework for learning reusable humanoid interaction skills from heterogeneous motion data. Central to our approach is a conditional interaction prior that models a context-dependent distribution over these skills within a shared discrete space. Our method is trained in three stages. We first learn physics-based motion-imitation policies that acquire grounded teacher behaviors from heterogeneous interaction data. We then distill these behaviors into a context-conditioned interaction prior that captures reusable motion structure across locomotion and manipulation. Finally, we initialize downstream task policies from the pretrained prior and adapt them through prior-regularized online RL post-training. Experiments on a diverse suite of humanoid interaction tasks show that our approach supports scene-aware locomotion, contact-rich object manipulation, and compositional behaviors such as environment-aware object transport and long-horizon skill sequencing, while producing smooth transitions and physically plausible motion.

papers.title: Unified Simulation of Lagrangian Particle Dynamics via Transformer
papers.authors: C. -C. Wang, Minghao Guo, Siyuan Chen, Heng Zhang, Mengdi Wang, Xingyu Ni, Hanson Sun, Kunyi Wang
papers.abstract: A unified simulator that can model diverse physical phenomena without solver-specific redesign is a long-standing goal across simulation science. We present a learning-based particle simulator built on a single transformer architecture to model cloth, elastic solids, Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids, granular materials, and molecular dynamics. Our model follows a prediction-correction design on a shared Lagrangian particle representation. An explicit predictor first advances particles under the known external forces, producing an intermediate state that captures externally driven motion but not inter-particle interactions. A learned corrector then predicts the residual position and velocity updates through three stages: a particle tokenizer that encodes local particle-particle, particle-boundary, and topology-guided interactions; a super-token encoder that hierarchically merges particle tokens into a compact set of super tokens via alternating self-attention and token merging; and a super-token decoder that lifts these super tokens back to particle resolution through cross-attention to predict per-particle position and velocity corrections. Progressive token merging reduces the attention cost at successive encoder layers by halving the token count at each level, and the decoder communicates through the compact super-token set rather than full particle-to-particle attention. Across the six dynamics categories, the same architecture generalizes to unseen materials, boundary configurations, initial conditions, and external forces. We further demonstrate downstream interactive control, inverse design, and learning from real-world manipulation data, reducing the need for per-phenomenon solver engineering.

papers.title: The Multivariate Feedback Particle Filter for State-dependent Multiplicative Noises and Its Application to Attitude and Pose Estimations
papers.authors: Jingyao You, Xue Luo
papers.abstract: Nonlinear filtering with state-dependent multiplicative measurement noise poses a notable challenge for spacecraft attitude determination and robotic pose estimation. This work develops the FPF-DM, a decomposition scheme for feedback particle filters tailored to this family of filtering problems. Extending prior decomposition techniques for additive noise and polynomial measurement models, the proposed method resolves the key difficulty that state-dependent multiplicative noise breaks the polynomial assumption and prevents Hermite spectral backward recursion for the weighted Poisson's equation. By measure transformation and importance reweighting, we incorporate the inverse measurement covariance into particle weights and rescale the feedback gain to restore the polynomial-form Poisson's equation, with the decomposition generalized to non-uniformly weighted mixtures for closed-form gain computation. This general FPF-DM is instantiated on quaternion and dual-quaternion manifolds for attitude tracking and point-cloud registration. Simulations on 4D attitude tracking and 8D point-cloud registration verify that the instantiated filters using only 10 particles achieve superior accuracy and computational performance relative to baseline filters.

papers.title: Testing World Models on Actions They Have Never Seen: Held-Out Plans, Forecast Accuracy and Price Rules in Retail
papers.authors: Karthik Iyer
papers.abstract: A world model is trusted to answer "what if": how its world responds to an action it has never seen. We give a test of that trust for any action-conditioned world model: actions held out of training by design and scored against a known answer; whether forecast accuracy predicts accuracy on those actions; and the same structure given to simpler models. We run it in retail, where the action is a price and promotion plan, across 2,853 fitted models. First, forecast accuracy is a fair guide between kinds of model (rank correlation with error on new plans 0.32 to 0.66) and a poor guide between versions of one world model: where merchants plan into high-demand weeks the link reverses, down to -0.69. Second, training the world model to learn the effect of actions (JEPA pretraining, a latent consistency check, adaptation at the plan date) leaves its error on new plans unchanged. Third, in generated worlds the recorded regular price and three price rules improve it. Given the same rules, a log-linear model is best when its curve can match the truth; in a world whose curve lies outside the rules, the world model with the rules is ahead of the log-linear model with the rules in 36 of 40 worlds, and does as well without its recurrent cell. On real data (Breakfast at the Frat, The Complete Journey and M5) the rules lower the world model's error on pure price cuts deeper than any it saw (0.63 to 0.56 on the Frat; 0.45 to 0.44, within chance, on The Complete Journey), but not on lasting price moves. Fourth, a small share of random test plans helps every model a little. In a generated dosing world, a stress test in a second domain, the first finding repeats, and the built-up drug level lowers the world model's error (2.86 to 1.91) though it still predicts only 0.12 to 0.32 of the true gain. The test carries to any domain where a world model is asked about actions outside its history.

papers.title: Terahertz Wireless Human-Like Sensing in the Microscopic Molecular Level
papers.authors: Huadóng Ma, D. W. Song, Zhan Zhang, Rui Lyu
papers.abstract: Perceptual intelligence is a fundamental research area in artificial intelligence, and human-like full-information perception represents a frontier direction in this field. Among the major challenges in this field, contactless human-like perception remains an open problem worldwide, and wireless sensing has emerged as a promising new technological pathway toward its realization. Previous studies have shown that the excitation of molecules by terahertz signals produces absorption spectra that encode molecular properties, thereby enabling microscopic, molecule-level sensing. In addition, the interactions between terahertz signals and objects can be exploited to identify material properties and surface geometries. This paper presents our exploration of terahertz wireless sensing for microscopic, molecule-level human-like sensing. We introduce the concept of a digital perceptual membrane that integrates terahertz signals with deep neural networks and develop a series of terahertz human-like sensing methods at the molecular level, including contactless taste, olfactory, and tactile sensing. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, providing a novel solution for realizing contactless human-like sensing. Finally, we discuss future research directions in terahertz wireless human-like sensing and highlight its potential applications in embodied intelligence, healthcare, food safety, and other fields.

papers.title: Technical Report of Mobile Manipulator Robot for Industrial Environments
papers.authors: Aria Dadnavi, Matin Jamshidi, Kian Khatibi, Shahriar Karimi Makhsous, Saina Najafi Shabestari, Seyed Sobhan Hosseini Hajibekandeh, Zahra Mahaam, Reyhane Mohasseli, et al.
papers.abstract: This paper presents the design and implementation of Auriga Robotics' mobile manipulator robot, developed at the Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory, Department of Electrical Engineering, Shahid Beheshti University. Hereafter, this platform is referred to as the @Work Robot. The robot targets industrial tasks, with an emphasis on improving efficiency in repetitive or hazardous work environments. It uses a 4-wheel Mecanum drive for omnidirectional movement and a 5-degree-of-freedom manipulator arm with a 3D-printed gripper for object handling and navigation. The electronics consist of custom PCB boards built around ESP32 microcontrollers, together with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX that handles high-level processing and real-time system control. On the software side, Hector SLAM provides mapping and localization, A* handles path planning, and YOLO performs real-time object detection. These modules draw on fused sensor data to deliver robust navigation and reliable collision avoidance. Overall, the system shows effective hardware-software integration, with consistent performance in autonomous navigation, object handling, and task execution in industrial-like settings.

papers.title: Task Convergent Flow Matching for Generative Robotics
papers.authors: Lorenzo Paiola, Maximilian Stölzle, Giorgio Grioli, Daniela Rus, Cosimo Della Santina
papers.abstract: Successful manipulation requires the manipulated objects to progress toward a desired task outcome. Generative policies can produce plausible robot motions without ensuring this progress, allowing successive action chunks to stall or undo earlier changes to the scene. We introduce a task-centric inference-time refinement framework for flow matching policies that evaluates candidate action chunks through parallel physics-based rollouts and searches for motions satisfying sufficient conditions for task convergence. Task-level performance funnels bound temporary regressions while requiring net progress over each chunk. We establish sufficient conditions under which repeated funnel satisfaction yields convergence throughout execution, and use interval-wise Lipschitz bounds to verify continuous-time funnel satisfaction from sampled rollouts. To accommodate contact-rich hybrid dynamics, we refine the flow's source seeds using derivative-free Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES), constrained to radial quantile bands of the source distribution to help retain the learned motion prior. This formulation supports both Euclidean and pose-valued Riemannian Flow Matching (RMFM) policies. On PushT and three-cube stacking, refinement raises success from 31.3% to 88.5% and from 77.0% to 86.0%. On PushT, whose coverage score responds continuously to the motion of the block, a learned funnel lowers the average maximum loss of achieved progress by 19% relative to constraining the endpoint of each chunk alone, at a similar success rate. With the radial band, 11.3% of the executed motion windows are out of distribution, a rate within the range of held-out demonstrations, compared with 34.1% for an unconstrained search.

papers.title: TRIDENT: Efficient Triple-Task Learning of Dehazing, Depth, and Uncertainty Estimation for Underwater 3-D Robot Visual Perception
papers.authors: Geonmo Yang, Younggun Cho
papers.abstract: Underwater visual systems often suffer from blurry textures and low color contrast due to the inevitable light propagation. These issues can significantly degrade the perception of stable robotic operations. In this paper, we introduce a novel learning-based sensing system that tackles the multidimensional vision tasks in underwater; concretely, we deal with image enhancement, depth estimation, and uncertainty for 3-D visual systems. Also, we propose a TRIDENT model in a fast and lightweight manner; TRIDENT consists of three parallelized decoders and one backbone structure for efficient feature sharing. In addition, it is designed to be trained to express complex parameterization. In experimental evaluation on several standard datasets, we demonstrate that TRIDENT significantly outperforms other existing methods on image enhancement and depth estimation. Despite performing three tasks, our model has better efficiency than the others for both memory size and inference time. Finally, our joint learning approach demonstrates robustness in feature matching and seamlessly extends from 2-D to 3-D vision tasks. papers.title: TCP4D: A Unified Tool-Center-Point Tracking and Generation Model for Robot Manipulation
papers.authors: Haosong Peng, Xiangyang Liu, Zhengshen Zhang, Yunfeng Fan, Tianyu Qi, Xin Xia, Yufeng Zhan, Wenchao Xu
papers.abstract: Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. The generator achieves 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin and outperforms well-established policy models on two real-world tasks, while joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.

papers.title: Surgical Intelligence Labs: a technical feasibility study of smartphone-based egocentric data capture and computational retargeting for robotic surgery
papers.authors: Mustafa Khan, Joao Bombardelli
papers.abstract: Surgical robotics could benefit from demonstrations of manual operating-room work, yet most existing surgical datasets emphasize endoscopic video or robot kinematics. We developed and evaluated a smartphone-based method for capturing first-person video, head pose, device motion and hand motion in a non-clinical simulation. Surgical Intelligence Labs is an iPhone application that records first-person video with synchronized ARKit camera pose and device motion. Apple Vision provides 21 two-dimensional hand keypoints per hand; an articulated model fits these keypoints in three dimensions and maps the fitted motion computationally to humanoid and bimanual robot models. Testing used two author-made, non-clinical recordings, including a 63-s bare-hand suturing simulation. The manuscript distinguishes implemented local capture functions from planned operating-room collection and de-identification workflows. In the 63-s suturing simulation, ARKit reported normal tracking for all 1,877 video frames and the phone pointed a mean 55° below the horizon. Both hands were detected in 97% of sampled frames and 99% of tracked hand observations retained a three-dimensional fit. These frame-level proportions describe a single temporally correlated sequence, not independent trials. Position-based retargeting reproduced median thumb-to-fingertip gaps within 2 mm of the fitted human-hand gaps; because gap matching is included in the position-based retargeting objective, this is a fitted-model geometric consistency check rather than independent validation. Numerical inverse kinematics solved all 300 G1 + and 200 WidowX deliberately reachable test targets (median position errors 1.1 and 0.35 mm, respectively). A consumer smartphone can capture synchronized first-person video, head pose, device motion and hand landmarks and map fitted hand motion to robot models computationally. This single-operator, non-clinical study establishes technical feasibility of the capture and processing pipeline; it does not establish absolute hand accuracy, generalizable performance, physical robot execution, policy learning or clinical readiness.

papers.title: SurgCBVR: A Multi-Domain Benchmark for Content-Based Surgical Video-to-Video Retrieval
papers.authors: Mohammad Eslami, Mousa Moradi, Negin Ghamsarian, Nazlee Zebardast, Jennifer L Lindsey, Sophia Y. Wang, Lucia Sobrin, Rishi P Singh, et al.
papers.abstract: Hospitals record thousands of hours of surgical video annually, yet these archives remain difficult to search by content. Surgeons cannot readily retrieve similar operations, complications, or workflow events. Existing surgical computer vision primarily produces labels rather than retrieving relevant videos. We introduce SurgCBVR, the first benchmark for content-based video-to-video retrieval in surgery. It integrates eight public datasets across four domains-ophthalmic, laparoscopic, robotic-assisted, and colonoscopy-covering six procedure types, 679 cases, and 76,489 clips (106 hours). SurgCBVR comprises two tiers: Scene, retrieving the same operative state across cases and sites, and Workflow, retrieving and localizing phase transitions and deviations. Scene includes 74,765 clips spanning 40 classes, three temporal granularities, and three playback speeds; Workflow contains 1,724 transition clips. Fixed clip lengths and frame counts, together with phase-classifier oracle and duration-only baselines, help assess label and timing shortcuts. We evaluate six generic and surgical foundation models, two video retrieval methods, and contrastive heads trained on SurgCBVR, using within-dataset, cross-dataset, and pooled-gallery retrieval restricted to the same procedure type. Frozen representations barely outperform a timing-only baseline, transition retrieval approaches chance, and trained heads lose up to half their accuracy across datasets. These findings expose substantial limitations in current video representations and establish SurgCBVR as a benchmark for advancing surgery-aware retrieval.

papers.title: Stochastic Diversity Windows: Diagnosing Noise Influence in Robotic Diffusion Sampling
papers.authors: Tina Lakhani, Jing Wu, Yu-Kun Lai, Ze Ji
papers.abstract: Diffusion models are increasingly adopted in robotics and control due to their capability to express multiple feasible solutions to a given task. However, the role of stochasticity in the diffusion model-sampler across denoising remains poorly understood. We introduce a per-timestep counterfactual diagnostic that tests how changing the sampled noise affects the final output. Across five model-sampler configurations spanning three robotics benchmarks, diverse architectures, domains, and conditioning mechanisms, we reveal highly varied temporal sensitivity profiles, where noise-induced deviations can amplify, partially contract, or undergo near-total attenuation downstream. From these profiles, we define stochastic diversity windows (SDWs): compact intervals that identify where sampler stochasticity has the strongest measured influence on the final output. Guided by these windows, we apply two heuristic interventions: targeted stochastic amplification, which increases sample diversity exploration of the solution space, and an SDW-hybrid sampler, which replaces DDPM steps with DDIM skips in low-impact regions, resulting in network evaluation reductions of up to 40-60% and wall-clock time by up to 85%, with no consistent changes detected in feasibility, cost, or diversity across held-out tasks.

papers.title: Spool: Low-Latency Streaming Inference for Hybrid Vision-Language Models
papers.authors: Rui Ning, Om Chabra, Hari Balakrishnan
papers.abstract: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. We present Spool, a training-free framework that caches per-frame state transformations and composes them efficiently as the window advances, removing expired frames from each recurrent layer's state without replaying frames through the backbone. Removal is exact within each layer; as with key-value eviction in attention, expired frames can retain residual influence through the cached inputs computed by earlier layers. We design a dedicated data structure and GPU kernels to achieve low caching and composition overhead. Across five open-source hybrid VLMs and four video reasoning benchmarks, Spool achieves the lowest p95 time-to-first-token in all 20 model-benchmark tests, reducing it by a geometric mean of $6.6\times$ over the faster of two recent vLLM baselines, while improving accuracy by 2.3 percentage points on average.

papers.title: SpatialCrafter: Single-Image World Modeling with Generative 3D Proxies
papers.authors: Chuan Fang, Lingteng Qiu, Yixun Liang, Rui Chen, Kunming Luo, Zhaohua Zheng, Tongyuan Bai, Fengqing Tian
papers.abstract: Explorable image-to-scene generation is essential for applications in gaming, robotics, and virtual reality. Existing methods based on video diffusion model (VDM) commonly rely on incomplete conditioning signals such as sparse point clouds or 2D panoramas, leading to stochastic hallucinations, long-term drifts and suboptimal 3D consistency. We present SpatialCrafter, a novel two-stage framework that addresses these issues by introducing a global 3D proxy for high-fidelity image-to-scene generation. Specifically, we decompose the generation process into global proxy generation and appearance refinement. For proxy generation, we propose a Point-anchored Sparse Structure (PaSS) Flow module that predicts a spatially aligned and geometrically consistent 3D proxy. For appearance refinement, we re-frame the VDM as a Generative Deferred Refiner which synthesizes high-frequency photorealistic details upon proxy-defined scene geometry. To better integrate the proxy with the pre-trained VDM, we introduce Parallel Geometry Injection and Proxy-Aware Corruption training strategies, which improve robustness to proxy artifacts without disrupting the pretrained generative manifold. Furthermore, as no suitable dataset exists for this explorable scene generation task, we construct a new large-scale dataset of 115K scenes. To the best of our knowledge, it is the first hybrid dataset for image-to-scene generation. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets show that SpatialCrafter outperforms state-of-the-art methods, mitigates long-term drift, and remains robust and consistent under rapid camera motion and extreme viewpoint changes. papers.title: SkiNet-Sim: Simulating Petri Nets with Data for the Verification and Validation of Controllers for Autonomous Systems
papers.authors: Baptiste Pelletier, Karen Godary
papers.abstract: A large amount of high-level Petri net formalisms has been investigated and deployed in academic settings over the past decades, but these deployments fail to reach practical applications, despite the strong guarantees they can bring to stakeholders. In particular, the lack of direct benefits from end-users reduces the appeal of Petri nets, both due to the overly simple classical Petri net formalism, and the overly specialized high-level formalisms, on top of state-space explosion issues. In this work, we investigate how a middle-ground could be reached, by separating the implementation-specific aspects of software or hardware behaviors, from the classical Petri net semantics. The goal is to benefit from the sought-after aspects of Petri nets, namely their simple firing semantic and model-checking capabilities, while still being able to augment their behavior to best reflect the modelled system. We present a formal model of Interpreted Petri nets with data-aware transitions and tokens. We illustrate this formalism by modelling the executive layer of a robotic system, and provide a lightweight tool to augment classical Petri nets for general purpose applications, as well as data-aware state-space exploration for model-checking. Their specialization in the context of autonomous robotics is showcased, with a complete industrial inspection mission use-case, to compare simulation and model-checking results between the classical and the new data-aware Petri net semantic.

papers.title: Simulation and Learning for Autonomous Surgical Robotics: From Language-Guided Blood Suction to End-to-End Suturing
papers.authors: Tleukhan Mussin
papers.abstract: Robot-assisted surgery has become increasingly common because it provides surgeons with improved precision, visualization, and dexterity. Existing surgical robots can reduce hand tremor and translate a surgeon's movements into precise instrument motion. However, these systems still depend heavily on direct human control, and their level of autonomous assistance remains limited. Increasing this assistance could reduce surgeons' workload and allow robots to handle repetitive or time-sensitive tasks. Achieving surgical autonomy is inherently more challenging than performing general robotic tasks because surgical environments are highly dynamic, involving deformable tissues and fluids, and require long procedures in which even a small mistake early on may affect everything that follows. Traditional motion-planning approaches can work well in carefully defined settings, but adapting them to a wide range of procedures would require extensive task-specific tuning, making them difficult to scale. Robot learning can reduce this dependence on hand-crafted techniques by learning from demonstrations or experience. However, it is limited by scarce real-world data, costly demonstrations, and the risks of trial-and-error training on physical tissue. This thesis therefore focuses on extending realistic surgical simulators and applying robot learning methods within these environments. The work considers blood suction in a changing soft tissue and fluid environment and suturing through deformable tissue. The first part investigates language-guided blood suction using vision-language-action (VLA) policies trained in simulation. The policies generate suction trajectories from natural-language instructions without requiring separate controllers for each command. The simulator is further extended to include deformable tissue, cutting, blood flow, and suction, enabling comparison between VLA models and a language-conditioned ACT policy. Results are promising, although the cutting and blood-flow scenarios still require physical validation. The second part builds on the existing GPU-accelerated CRESSim-MPM soft-tissue engine by adding a PBD suture model and two-way coupling between the suture and MPM tissue. Reinforcement-learning agents trained entirely in the resulting environment learn needle insertion, driving, and extraction, achieving 80\% success for insertion and 68\% for extraction under the strictest evaluation threshold. These results demonstrate the extended simulator's potential as a platform for robotic suturing research. The final part further extends this platform to autonomous end-to-end suturing using a hierarchical five-phase framework. Comparing ACT with asymmetric Residual Fine-Tuning (aResFiT), aResFiT completes 38 of 50 phase trials, compared with 29 of 50 for the original imitation-learning policies, while reducing entry and exit errors. Initial transfer to a physical da Vinci Research Kit also demonstrates that simulation-trained policies can transfer to real hardware, while still some sim-to-real challenges remain. Overall, this thesis contributes extensions to surgical simulation environments and learning frameworks for language-guided blood suction and multi-phase suturing. The results support simulation-first development while showing that physical validation, broader randomization, improved calibration, and learning methods that correct motion are required before clinical usage.

papers.title: Similar Is Not Useful: Selecting In-Context Demonstrations by Closed-Loop Utility
papers.authors: Jiachen Li, Zhigen Zhao, Shihao Li, Dongmei Chen, Long Chen, Zhuo Xu
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) policies fill their context with the demonstrations whose frames look most like the current observation under frozen DINOv2 embeddings. We ask whether visual similarity selects the demonstrations that make the policy succeed. For a frozen retrieval-augmented VLA (RICL on $π_0$-FAST, LIBERO), we make the demonstration pool swappable at run time and score each demonstration's utility by regressing the closed-loop success of 60 fixed-size pools on their membership. On initial states disjoint from those used for scoring, pools of the five highest-utility demonstrations succeed on 66.4% of 760 paired episodes across 19 tasks, pools of the five most similar on 55.7%, and random pools on 55.5%. Utility beats similarity by 10.8 points ($p=3.2\times10^{-6}$; positive on 15 of 18 untied tasks), including on 12 tasks the policy was never primed on, and similarity-selected pools do no better than random ($+0.1$ points). Within a task, a pool's visual similarity to the test scenes tracks its success at Spearman 0.10; across tasks, similarity separates tasks whose scenes differ and falls to chance when two tasks share a scene. The gain comes from on-task closed-loop evidence: best-of-ten direct search over pools recovers two-thirds of it with 100 rollouts. Against the shipped 20-demonstration pool, utility-curated pools of five lead by 7.0 points over 560 paired episodes from two evaluation runs ($p=0.006$), and utility-ordered retrieval inside the full pool leads by 4.5 points ($p=0.055$).

papers.title: Sim2CBF: From Forward Simulations to Implicit Control Barrier Function Safety Filtering without Model Derivatives
papers.authors: Luzia Knoedler, Yihan Liu, Shaohang Han, Yifei Dong, Jana Tumova
papers.abstract: Failure avoidance in complex robot-environment interactions is challenging because the underlying dynamics are difficult to model accurately, and available predictive models may not provide reliable derivatives. We present Sim2CBF, a failure-avoidance framework that solves the Control Barrier Function (CBF)-Safety Filter (SF) optimization problem using only forward-model evaluations, thereby avoiding differentiation of the predictive model. Specifically, we approximate the CBF constraint using finite differences and local linear interpolation over sampled control inputs while preserving failure-avoidance guarantees. The underlying CBF is implicit and constructed from backup-policy rollouts, enabling the use of expressive predictive models such as physics-based simulators and learned world models. Compared with purely sampling-based SFs, our formulation requires fewer control samples and yields less conservative behavior than direct nominal-backup blending. We evaluate Sim2CBF in simulation, hardware box-toppling, and vision-based control tasks, demonstrating its applicability to contact-rich and learned dynamics, as well as its adaptability to changes in the predictive model.

papers.title: Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Robust Synthesis of Signal Temporal Logic Specifications
papers.authors: Philip Smith, Kevin Leahy
papers.abstract: Signal Temporal Logic is a popular framework for describing a robotic system's goals. Once described using a temporal logic framework, synthesis turns the goals into actual steps for the robots to follow. Currently, the state of the art for sound and complete synthesis is using Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP), which struggles on long time horizons and large environments, preventing the construction of guaranteed safe plans for long deployments. This paper introduces a new synthesis method using Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) which scales better for long deployments and adapts to environmental changes more quickly. We do this by introducing an encoding method for STL into SMT constraints, and an encoding method for discrete-time dynamical systems modeled as a transition system. We then conduct an empirical comparison of our SMT based methods against the state of the art MILP based methods. Results show that for this class of problems, SMT is an effective encoding strategy that performs the best on long time horizon tasks.

papers.title: SR-VLA: Stall-Reduced VLA Execution via Predicted-Input Lookahead and Selective KV Cache Repair
papers.authors: Tao Zhang, Yi Zhong, Jinhao Ruan, Yipeng Gao, Linfeng Zhong, Youming Yang, Yuan Wang
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies incur control stalls when inference blocks the next action chunk. Asynchronous early inference can hide latency, but its results may be inconsistent with the arriving actual inputs. Unconditional reuse risks acting on mismatched inputs, whereas full recomputation discards useful precomputation. We propose SR-VLA, combining predicted-input lookahead with selective KV cache repair. During current chunk execution, a lightweight action-conditioned predictor generates next-boundary visual observations and proprioceptive state. These predictions, together with the task instruction, drive the frozen VLA to precompute a speculative KV cache and action chunk. After real inputs are available to VLA, predicted--real differences and task conditions determine whether to accept the action chunk or trigger selective KV repair. On LIBERO, SR-VLA achieves $2.67\times$ and $1.27\times$ query speedups over the respective synchronous $π_{0.5}$ and OpenVLA-OFT baselines, while maintaining competitive average task success rates. Under target-motion perturbation, success remains baseline-comparable, with $1.52\times$--$1.93\times$ query speedup.

papers.title: SPICE: Stochastic Policy for Interaction in Cluttered Environments
papers.authors: Nidhi Parayil, Benjamin Greenland, Thierry Peynot, Chris Lehnert
papers.abstract: Agricultural tasks such as harvesting and pruning require robots to reach through dense foliage, where contact is often unavoidable and vision is obstructed. Intermittent contact creates an imbalance between free-space and contact-rich observations, complicating the learning of contact-responsive behaviours. We present SPICE, a tactileconditioned diffusion policy for reaching targets in dense plant canopies using tactile sensing as the sole environmental feedback. SPICE exhibits three behaviours: moving through compliant foliage, manoeuvring around partially obstructing stems, and manipulating branches that block the target path. To the best of our knowledge, SPICE is the first tactile-conditioned diffusion policy for target reaching through physically cluttered plant canopies. Across over 180 real-robot trials, SPICE was evaluated against tactile-conditioned, image-conditioned, and reactive-control baselines. Spatial tactile information and explicit contact conditioning proved important, with SPICE achieving 95% branch-manoeuvring success versus 45% for the strongest tactile baseline. SPICE also achieved branch manipulation beyond the reactive controller and remained effective under visual occlusion, where the image-conditioned DP failed. Zero-shot transfer across 40 trials on unseen tomato and lime plants achieved 87.5% success rate. These results demonstrate the potential of tactile-conditioned generative policies for interaction in visually occluded plant environments.

papers.title: SCRIPT: Scalable Diffusion Policy with Multi-stage Training for Language-driven Physics-Based Humanoid Control
papers.authors: Jingyan Zhang, Han Liang, Ruichi Zhang, Bin Li, Juze Zhang, Xin Chen, Jingya Wang, Lan Xu
papers.abstract: Controlling physics-based humanoids from natural-language instructions is a critical step toward general-purpose embodied agents. However, existing methods remain constrained by a tension between semantic expressiveness and physical feasibility, often failing to jointly achieve faithful instruction following, high-quality motion, and stable long-horizon control. We propose SCRIPT, a scalable diffusion policy with a multi-stage training framework for language-driven physics-based humanoid control. The core of SCRIPT is a Joint Action-State-Text Diffusion Transformer (JAST-DiT), which represents actions, physical states, and text as dedicated token streams and couples them through joint attention, enabling direct interaction between language semantics and control dynamics. To stabilize autoregressive control, we introduce a nonlinear history conditioning mechanism, which preserves the dense recent context and samples increasingly sparse cues from long-term history. Beyond supervised imitation pre-training, we propose a post-training stage, further improving the performance using Reinforcement Learning with Hybrid Rewards (RLHR). By injecting learnable noise into the flow-sampling process, RLHR effectively improves motion quality and instruction following within closed-loop simulations using hybrid physical feedback and text rewards. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate that SCRIPT outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods, with gains across text alignment, motion quality, and physical realism metrics. Furthermore, scaling studies on the 1200-hour MotionMillion dataset demonstrate consistent performance gains with model scaling, highlighting SCRIPT's robust scalability for large-scale pre-training. Our code will be publicly available for future research.

papers.abstract: As embodied agents become central to VR, telepresence, and digital human applications, their motion must go beyond speech-aligned gestures: agents should turn toward users, respond to their movement, and maintain natural gaze. Current methods lack this spatial awareness. We close this gap with the first real-time, fully causal method for spatially-aware conversational motion, deployable on a streaming VR headset. Given a user's position and dyadic audio, our approach produces full-body motion that aligns gestures with speech while orienting the agent according to the user. Our architecture combines a causal transformer-based VAE with interleaved latent tokens for streaming inference and a flow matching model conditioned on user trajectory and audio. To support varying gaze preferences, we introduce a gaze scoring mechanism with classifier-free guidance to decouple learning from control: the model captures natural spatial alignment from data, while users can adjust eye contact intensity at inference time. On the Embody 3D dataset, our method achieves state-of-the-art motion quality at over 300 FPS -- 3x faster than non-causal baselines -- while capturing the subtle spatial dynamics of natural conversation. We validate our approach on a live VR system, bringing spatially-aware conversational agents to real-time deployment. Please see https://evonneng.github.io/sarah/ for details.

papers.title: Robotic-assisted surgery and artificial intelligence in female infertility: a clinical maturity framework for evidence-based integration
papers.authors: Mahsa Motamed, Sadaf Saket, Masoud Saadat Fakhr, Shahrzade Valizadehashenaabad, Poorya Gholami, Zahra Amini, Koosha Amiri, Mona Abediasl
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Female infertility often requires coordinated diagnostic, surgical, and assisted reproductive strategies. Robotic-assisted surgery (RAS) may facilitate selected fertility-preserving procedures, while artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly applied to reproductive imaging, embryo assessment, ovarian stimulation, prognosis, and clinical decision support. The clinical evidence for both technologies is uneven, and direct AI integration into robotic infertility surgery remains early. Main body This critical review evaluates current evidence for RAS in myomectomy, tubal reanastomosis, endometriosis surgery, adhesiolysis, ovarian surgery, and selected reconstructive procedures, alongside clinically relevant AI applications in assisted reproduction and reproductive imaging. RAS may offer technical advantages in complex cases through enhanced visualization, instrument articulation, ergonomics, and suturing, but superiority over expert conventional laparoscopy for cumulative live birth, time to pregnancy, ovarian reserve preservation, and cost-effectiveness remains insufficiently established. AI can improve standardization and prediction, but many models remain retrospective, internally validated, incompletely calibrated, or insufficiently tested for clinical utility. We propose a clinical maturity framework that distinguishes current surgeon-controlled RAS from research-stage AI support and speculative autonomous surgery. The most plausible near-term AI-RAS integration is clinician-supervised support for preoperative imaging, surgical difficulty prediction, intraoperative video analytics, robotic skill assessment, postoperative fertility prognosis, and sequencing of surgery and assisted reproductive technology. Conclusion AI and RAS may become complementary components of female infertility care, but routine integrated use requires multicenter prospective validation, standardized infertility-specific outcomes, transparent AI reporting, patient-centered evaluation, regulatory oversight, and assessment of cost and equity.

papers.title: RoboTeam: Benchmarking Vision-Based Multi-Agent Control of Many Robot Arms in Real Time
papers.authors: Changxuan Fan, Zhongwei Xie, Boyi Zhang, Shaoli Hu, Chang Xu, Xiyu Ren, Yufei Li, Qiao Xiao, et al.

Existing benchmarks fall short in three ways: most test one or two arms on short tasks, many pause the world while the agent thinks, and many give it ground-truth object positions. We present RoboTeam, a simulated benchmark where agents control 4 to 16 robot arms in real time from camera images alone. Its 36 tasks are long jobs that the arms must do together, such as passing timbers or building a picture from hundreds of cubes. We start from the most flexible agent system, the adaptive system, where one agent decides when to fork delegates. With it, gpt-6.1-sol and opus-5.5 complete 28 and 27 tasks, and four other models at most 3. But at a high price: a typical task takes gpt-6.1-sol 3.5 hours and 218 million input tokens, and a third of its steps fail at least once and must be retried. We then compare it with three fixed systems: single-agent, hierarchical, and decentralized. All four complete a similar number of tasks but differ in time and tokens. The hierarchical and decentralized systems are faster but use up to 1.9 times the tokens, and the single agent uses fewer tokens but takes 1.6 times as long, so the adaptive system lies between them. Even so, no model or system is yet fast, cheap, and reliable at once. RoboTeam measures these limits where earlier benchmarks cannot: long multi-arm jobs, camera images only, and a world that never pauses.

papers.title: Risk Density RRT$^*$: Planning in the Space of Probability
papers.authors: Lorenzo Paiola, Giorgio Grioli, Antonio Bicchi
papers.abstract: Planning under uncertainty is a fundamental problem in robotics. While much of the literature seeks minimum-cost paths subject to probabilistic constraints, this paper instead considers collision probability, or risk classically defined as probability times severity, directly as the planning objective. We propose Risk Density RRT$^*$ (RD-RRT$^*$), an extension of RRT$^*$ for high-level planning in environments with deterministic and uncertain obstacles. RD-RRT$^*$ builds on Risk Density, a functional that evaluates a continuous path as a whole and provides a tractable approximation of its collision probability. The framework also supports severity-weighted risk and a hybrid variant that adds a path-length penalty, balancing risk and geometric efficiency while regularizing exploration in low-density regions. We validate the method across a wide range of scenarios. The results show that RD-RRT$^*$ consistently finds paths with lower estimated collision probability by optimizing a global risk-based objective. We further demonstrate the fidelity of the underlying approximation through Monte Carlo simulations. Finally, we discuss how the topological structure induced by Risk Density may provide a useful representation of the environment and offer insights into risk-aware planning.

papers.title: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model
papers.authors: Jiaqi Wu, Yongqi Dong, Yijie Zhong, Maple Shao, Yide Tao, Linsen Cai, Weize Cai, Hai L. Vu, et al.
papers.abstract: In automated driving, world models provide future scene predictions for evaluating candidate trajectories, but fixed selection rules may not capture scene-dependent trade-offs. The framework uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals. A context-conditioned ranking network learns candidate preferences from feedback obtained by evaluating local perturbations of the selected trajectories. At inference, the selector combines learned preference and predicted risk ranks using fixed weights and returns the selected candidate trajectory without modification. Fine-tuning updates 16,106 parameters across the actor and critic, while the deployed selector retains only the 11,725-parameter ranking network, with the residual branch and critic used exclusively during training. In open-loop evaluation on the nuScenes validation set, the method reduces average Euclidean trajectory error (L2) by 3.99% relative to the RiskWorld model baseline without RL-based selection. Under matched budgets for feedback accesses and actor updates, residual exploration reduces L2 by 0.83% relative to the categorical PPO variant trained without residuals. The method also maintains lower L2 than RiskWorld when risk features are removed or shuffled.

papers.title: RefCloth: Transferable Adversarial Tablecloths for Vision-Language-Action Models

papers.title: Recoverability, Not Invariance: Certified Safety for Robots at the Limits of Performance
papers.authors: Thomas A. Berrueta, Joshua D. Ibrahim, Gilchrist X. Johnson, John Lathrop, Soon-Jo Chung
papers.abstract: Safety certification in robotics typically rests on forward invariance of the deployed controller, a property that demands high-fidelity models at the edge of the operating envelope, exactly where models are least reliable and robots perform best. As a result, many of the behaviors we most want robots to run, from learned policies to aggressive maneuvers at the limits of traction, cannot be certified at all. We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that resolves this tension by certifying a robot's ability to reengage a trusted recovery mode rather than the invariance of a deployed behavior. We prove that switching to the recovery mode from anywhere inside a certified tube guarantees exponential convergence, even under disturbances and model error. To decide when to switch, we derive the contraction insertion gradient, the first-order effect of a recovery insertion on the certificate, and embed it in a switching-time program in which feasibility alone guarantees safety and optimality only shapes performance. To supply the certificates, we develop sequential convex synthesis that monotonically grows the certified tube toward the exact viability kernel. We validate our approach in simulated quadrotor flight through uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms invariance-based safety filters, and in hardware deployments aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, where it repeatedly recovers the car from an aggressive raceline at the limits of handling in the rain. Recoverability provides a certified exit strategy, extending formal safety guarantees to aggressive, learned, and experimental behaviors without requiring their invariance.

papers.title: Reconfiguring Procedural Knowledge for Compositional Robot Skill Adaptation
papers.authors: Daehee Lee, Dongsu Lee, Sanghyun Ahn, Minjong Yoo, Honguk Woo
papers.abstract: General-purpose behavior models increasingly internalize broad procedural knowledge during training, making their adaptation to new goals and skill interfaces less a problem of learning entirely new behaviors than of reconfiguring existing competence. We study this capability as reconfigurability, the ability to realize new behaviors by cost-efficiently restructuring existing components and relations under sparse governing information, where task specifications provide high-level goals and procedure specifications expose a limited set of reusable factors, leaving the concrete bindings and compositions required for execution underdetermined. We propose RecPo, a framework that represents skills task-agnostically through multiple procedure views and materializes executable skill sequences by composing stored transitions to realize task-specific changes. RecPo maintains a procedure knowledge base of skill-induced transitions, with each view exposing a reusable factor and preserving local skill connectivity. At deployment, it interprets task specifications through the same views and resolves the resulting compositional queries over the stored relations to bind skills for execution. On long-horizon tasks in an extended Franka Kitchen benchmark, RecPo achieves 91.9% ordered completion with 1.0 ms of task inference per episode across varying procedure support and task-record sparsity. papers.title: ReLAP: Latent Action Pretraining through Recurrent Video Prediction in JEPA Space
papers.authors: R. Gnana Praveen, Ali Rouzbayani, Zhiying Jiang, Bidhan Roy
papers.abstract: Videos provide a rich source of physical interaction for learning robot behavior without action annotations, yet effective latent actions must capture not only local transitions but also how those transitions evolve over time. We introduce ReLAP, a latent-action pretraining framework that couples local transition learning with recurrent multi-step prediction in a frozen JEPA representation space. A shared inverse dynamics model infers compact continuous latent actions from adjacent observations, while a latent world model recurrently predicts the future JEPA features. Because each predicted feature becomes the context for the next transition, errors at later steps backpropagate through the rollout to earlier latent actions, encouraging temporally coherent dynamics beyond pairwise reconstruction. We transfer this representation to a vision-language model using two complementary objectives: latent distillation from the frozen inverse teacher and recurrent future-feature prediction through the frozen latent world model. The resulting policy is then adapted to robot demonstrations with action flow matching. At deployment, the explicit latent-action and world-model branches are removed, and the fine-tuned VLM predicts physical actions directly, reducing inference complexity. With only 11M pretraining samples and 1.06B trainable parameters, ReLAP achieves 97.9% on standard LIBERO and 70.0% over zero-shot LIBERO-Plus perturbations. On the LARY latent-action benchmark, ReLAP ranks second in both mean regression error and mean classification accuracy among the compared methods. These results demonstrate that recurrent action-free latent action pretraining can learn compact, temporally structured, and transferable representations for downstream robot control.

papers.title: RageVLA: Augmentation-Trained Perception and Action for State-of-the-Art Robustness on LIBERO
papers.authors: Amrit Lal Singh, Smarak Kanjilal
papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models look saturated on LIBERO, yet most of them fall apart on LIBERO-PRO as soon as an object moves or the instruction asks for something new. We argue that what is missing is not scale but decoupling. In these policies, what to do is tied to where things were during training, to the scene around them and to the wording of the instruction. We cut these ties in two places. In the data, LIBERO demonstrations are re-arranged by general rules: every object and fixture is moved and rotated, tasks are carried into other environments and onto other surfaces, and every instruction is paraphrased. In the policy, a perception engine on frozen DINOv3 features, trained on this augmented data, hands the action model the scene in decoupled form: a list of objects with their positions, and a compact code of what the gripper is looking at, next to image and instruction embeddings from TinyCLIP. A flow-matching diffusion transformer, trained from scratch, acts on this view. We call this combination of Robust Augmentation and Grounded Encoding RageVLA. With 0.21 billion parameters, RageVLA sets a new state of the art on LIBERO-PRO among VLA policies, scoring 0.72 against 0.53 for the best published model, and a larger variant reaches 0.73. Two further tests on LIBERO-Object show that the policy acts on what it perceives. When the object positions it is given are shuffled while the camera images stay correct, its success falls from 0.965 to 0.215. When the target object is displaced by 28 cm, it still succeeds in 0.865 of the episodes, where $π_{0.5}$, run through the same harness, succeeds in 0.105.

papers.title: ROSMonitoring in Action: Runtime Monitoring and Enforcement for ROS 2 Actions
papers.authors: Giacomo Paltrinieri, Angelo Ferrando
papers.abstract: Robotic applications often rely on long-running operations, such as navigation, manipulation, and inspection, which in ROS~2 are commonly implemented as actions. The results show approximately linear growth in monitoring cost with repeated action invocations under a fixed workload, while larger action workloads and a greater number of configured clientâserver pairs introduce additional overhead. These results characterise the scaling behaviour of the current implementation under the tested sequential workloads while highlighting the main performance limitations of the current synchronous implementation.

papers.title: RFW-S: Everyday Deformable Objects with Independent Simulation Verification
papers.authors: Jiarui Guo, Saining Zhang, Jiaying Wan, Jiawei Weng, Junhao Chen, Rui Zhang, Yuanbo Lyu, Zhiheng Lee, et al.

We develop an automated pipeline integrating reference-guided 3D generation, structure-aware physical modeling, and LLM-assisted parameter estimation and calibration. To ensure physical reliability, we introduce an independent simulation verification framework that evaluates object behaviors under interactions distinct from those used for parameter calibration. papers.title: RESCUE Jumper: A Centimeter-Scale Rolling and Jumping Robot for Search and Rescue
papers.authors: Kiran Marques, Shashwat Singh, Ben D'Ambrosia, Zeynep Temel, Melisa Orta Martinez
papers.abstract: Centimeter-scale robots are promising for urban search and rescue because they can enter confined spaces that are inaccessible or unsafe for humans. However, their small size limits obstacle traversal after deployment. This paper presents the RESCUE Jumper, a 125 g mobile robot with a 6.2 cm width and 6.2 cm diameter wheels that combines ground rolling with jumping to traverse steps and gaps that exceeds its rolling capability. The RESCUE Jumper uses its two actuators for both rolling mode and jumping by reversing the direction of wheel motion. Forward wheel motion enables rolling, while reverse wheel motion winds a spring steel tail to store elastic potential energy and release it for jumping. The RESCUE Jumper varies tail winding speed to control jump direction, transitioning from backward to forward jumps as winding speed increases from 0.75 rad/s to 8.73 rad/s. The launch angle of the jumps ranges from 45 degree to -11 degree with respect to the vertical axis, reaching a maximum height of 9.2 cm and a maximum lateral displacement of 11.2 cm. We model the winding speed-dependent jumping behavior in three phases: tail release to determine the contact point and robot orientation, tail straightening until liftoff, and ballistic flight to predict jump height and lateral displacement. Finally, qualitative tests highlight the robot's locomotion in cluttered, real-world environments. The model and experiments presented in this work can inform future designs of space-constrained jump mechanisms in centimeter-scale robots for search and rescue and inspection in unstructured environments.

papers.title: Proximity3D: Shape from Capacitive Proximity on Sensing Manifold

papers.title: Progress Predicts Policy
papers.authors: Licheng Zhong, Gim Hee Lee
papers.abstract: A task specifies how the world should change, while a policy specifies what the robot should do. We introduce Progress Predicts Policy (PPP), which learns a language-conditioned scalar field through the commands induced by its differential. We obtain action conditioning by composing a latent progress field with a shared world model and read its action gradient at a fixed reference command. Continuous commands scale this gradient by a learned positive gain, while discrete commands use finite differences of the same scalar. This yields a hybrid policy without a separate action head or iterative search. Fitting demonstration progress values alone does not ensure that action gradients align with expert commands. PPP trains the induced commands by imitation and uses double backpropagation for the continuous gradient readout to shape the field's local control geometry. Demonstration timing calibrates field values on observed states without additional annotation. The continuous readout remains learnable without progress labels but these timing-derived targets support progress monitoring during execution. Experiments in simulated and real robot manipulation show that PPP outperforms behavioral cloning under a shared architecture.

papers.authors: Gunjari Chakraborty, Yasmin Rafiq, Hazel M. Taylor, Marie Farrell

Temporal analysis showed that 70.1% of the unique FRETISH requirements use either immediate-response or ordering constraints (immediately or before), while formalisation also exposed relationships between requirements across HRT taxonomy categories. We further analyse the formal semantics and realisability of the resulting requirements. The results show that HRT classification and formalisation provide complementary views: the taxonomy captures the teamwork concern represented by a requirement, while FRETISH makes the required behaviour explicit. papers.title: Plausible Videos Can Lead to Poor Decisions: Diagnosing and CURE-ing World Models for Planning
papers.authors: Raphael C. Kim, Michele Santacatterina, Jingsen Zhu, Ramin Zabih
papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly used as world models for planning, yet a world model that makes plausible, realistic-looking videos that are consistent with the training data can produce poor decisions. We introduce CURE (Certify, Upweight, Rollout, Explore), a certificate-guided technique that assesses whether a world model can be trusted for planning and determines what to do next: whether to upweight the training data to debias the model; roll out more samples at test time; or explore by collecting new data where support (how well the training data cover the planner's decisions) is missing. We deploy CURE across multiple domains, spanning simulated physics based on PhyWorld, MuJoCo arm control, and Language-Table pushing in simulation and on real videos. The decisions our certificate trusts have lower regret than those it does not (e.g., 0.06 vs. 0.38 on Language-Table sim and 0.07 vs. 0.38 on MuJoCo contact), whereas video perceptual quality does not identify good decisions. By focusing on decision quality rather than perceptual quality, CURE lowers regret over the best pessimistic decision rule by 10-25% across support levels, and over world-action models, search and policy learning by 41-64%, given the same data.

papers.title: Pixel is All You Need
papers.authors: Jie Chu, Haoting Shi, Fucheng Zhang, Jiawei Liu, Junwei Liao, Ying Wen, Muning Wen
papers.abstract: Text, images, audio, touch, and even robot actions can, in principle, all be rendered onto a single canvas, suggesting an ambitious goal of unifying all modalities within vision. Language provides the natural first test. To subsume it, a visual model must reason directly over text in pixels. Across a wide range of image, video, and unified multimodal generators, however, we find that their visual generation modules cannot perform symbolic reasoning over text on the canvas. They succeed only when an underlying text module or prompt rewriter already supplies the answer, effectively reducing the generator to a mere renderer, a limitation that post-training does little to resolve. To test whether this failure stems from pixels themselves or from current training paradigms, we train a family of purely pixel-space generative models from scratch without any text pathway. With images as their sole input and output, these models read questions, write intermediate steps, and produce answers directly on the canvas. Remarkably, they exhibit hallmark behaviors of large language models. Performance improves predictably with scale following a power law. Writing intermediate steps frame by frame substantially outperforms single-frame answering, echoing chain-of-thought, while reinforcement-learning post-training further strengthens reasoning. Moreover, sharing one canvas allows the same model to reason across modalities, a capability that text-only language models lack. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic study of these phenomena in purely pixel-space generative models free of text tokens.

papers.title: PhyVGGT: Feed-Forward Articulated Object Reconstruction from Monocular Videos
papers.authors: Qi Shao, Zhihao Cao, Shuhao Zhai, Anh Nguyen, Hong Liang, Baoru Huang, Liang Li
papers.abstract: Reconstructing an articulated object with its 3D movable parts, joint parameters and unseen articulation states from an uncalibrated monocular video is essential for robot manipulation and interactive digital twins. Existing per-scene optimisation methods require minutes to hours and external depth or camera poses, whereas feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct dense point maps in one pass without segmenting movable parts or inferring joints. Even on these monocular point maps, regressing or fitting continuous joints directly fails on casual videos, since cross-frame attention blurs moving part boundaries in deep layers, underestimates motion along the viewing ray and leaves continuous axes ill-conditioned under small opening angles. To address these challenges, we propose PhyVGGT, a single-pass framework on a frozen 3D foundation model that anchors moving-part matching and closed-form joint estimation to the undistorted geometry of the stationary base. First, our Part and Motion Decoder fuses intermediate per-frame tokens with global tokens and references part queries to a static-base query to segment 3D parts, align point maps on the static base and predict learned Bingham priors. Second, our Kinematic Inference Layer fits an orthogonal Manhattan frame to static surface normals, selects the joint axis in closed form under a Bingham posterior combining pairwise motion scatter with the learned priors, and solves a linear system for the hinge pivot to drive unseen states. Trained solely on synthetic data, PhyVGGT achieves state-of-the-art monocular performance across five benchmarks, outperforming FAMOS and monocular ArtiPoint, surpassing posed RGB-D ArtiPoint in median error, and running in 6.8 s per 48-frame video against hours of per-scene optimisation in Articulat3D. Across 30 methods and 24 seeds, PANINI achieves the best mean rank but is not statistically distinguishable from strong generic optimizers. Its main demonstrated advantage is therefore structural rather than optimization performance: grammar-generated designs are legal by construction, and coordinated limb placement produces 95% jointly feasible edits, compared with 55% for range-constrained resampling and none for flat parameterization in 6,000 draws. papers.title: PAct: Part-Decomposed Single-View Articulated Object Generation
papers.authors: Qingming Liu, Xinyue Yao, Shuyuan Zhang, Yueci Deng, Guiliang Liu, Zhen Liu, Kui Jia
papers.abstract: Articulated objects are central to interactive 3D applications, including embodied AI, robotics, and VR/AR, where functional part decomposition and kinematic motion are essential. Yet producing high-fidelity articulated assets remains difficult to scale because it requires reliable part decomposition and kinematic rigging. Existing approaches largely fall into two paradigms: optimization-based reconstruction or distillation, which can be accurate but often takes tens of minutes to hours per instance, and inference-time methods that rely on template or part retrieval, producing plausible results that may not match the specific structure and appearance in the input observation. We introduce a part-centric generative framework for articulated object creation that synthesizes part geometry, composition, and articulation under explicit part-aware conditioning. Our representation models an object as a set of movable parts, each encoded by latent tokens augmented with part identity and articulation cues. Conditioned on a single image, the model generates articulated 3D assets that preserve instance-level correspondence while maintaining valid part structure and motion. The resulting approach avoids per-instance optimization, enables fast feed-forward inference, and supports controllable assembly and articulation, which are important for embodied interaction. Experiments on common articulated categories (e.g., drawers and doors) show improved input consistency, part accuracy, and articulation plausibility over optimization-based and retrieval-driven baselines, while substantially reducing inference time.
